entries.66f29747852814187b0d23c4ba086ac283d79344: <div sID="gen29519" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Acts.13" sID="Acts.13"/> <div eID="gen29519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29520" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29521" type="x-p"/> We have not yet met with any things concerning the spreading of the gospel to the Gentiles which bears any proportion to the largeness of that commission, "Go, and disciple all nations." The door was opened in the baptizing of Cornelius and his friends; but since then we had the gospel preached to the Jews only, <reference osisRef="Acts.11.19">ch. xi. 19</reference>. It should seem as if the light which began to shine upon the Gentile world had withdrawn itself. But here in this chapter that work, that great good work, is revived in the midst of the years; and though the Jews shall still have the first offer of the gospel made to them, yet, upon their refusal, the Gentiles shall have their share of the offer of it. Here is, I. The solemn ordination of Barnabas and Saul, by divine direction, to the ministry, to the great work of spreading the gospel among the nations about (and it is probable that other apostles or apostolical men dispersed themselves by order from Christ, upon the same errand, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1-Acts.13.3">ver. 1-3</reference>). II. Their preaching the gospel in Cyprus, and the opposition they met with there from Elymas the sorcerer, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.4-Acts.13.13">ver. 4-13</reference>. III. The heads of a sermon which Paul preached to the Jews at Antioch in Pisidia, in their synagogue, which is given us as a specimen of what they usually preached to the Jews, and the method they took with them, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.14-Acts.13.41">ver. 14-41</reference>. IV. The preaching of the gospel to the Gentiles at their request, and upon the Jews' refusal of it, wherein the apostles justified themselves against the displeasure which the Jews conceived at it, and God owned them, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.42-Acts.13.49">ver. 42-49</reference>. V. The trouble which the infidel Jews gave to the apostles, which obliged them to remove to another place (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.50-Acts.13.52">ver. 50-52</reference>), so that the design of this chapter is to show how cautiously, how gradually, and with what good reason the apostles carried the gospel into the Gentile world, and admitted the Gentiles into the church, which was so great an offence to the Jews, and which Paul is so industrious to justify in his epistles.
entries.ac77f161ace61be5c342da72c350ac3c1e2c922c: <div eID="gen29521" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29520" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Mission of Paul and Barnabas.</title> <div sID="gen29522" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <hi type="super">2</hi> As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. 3 And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid <hi type="italic">their</hi> hands on them, they sent <hi type="italic">them</hi> away. <div eID="gen29522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29523" type="x-p"/> We have here a divine warrant and commission to Barnabas and Saul to go and preach the gospel among the Gentiles, and their ordination to that service by the imposition of hands, with fasting and prayer. <div eID="gen29523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29524" type="x-p"/> I. Here is an account of the present state of the church at Antioch, which was planted, <reference osisRef="Acts.11.20">ch. xi. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen29524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29525" type="x-p"/> 1. How well furnished it was with good ministers; there were there <hi type="italic">certain prophets and teachers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.1">v. 1</reference>), men that were eminent for gifts, graces, and usefulness. Christ, when he <hi type="italic">ascended on high,</hi> gave <hi type="italic">some prophets and some teachers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Eph. iv. 11</reference>); these were both. Agabus seems to have been a prophet and not a teacher, and many were teachers who were not prophets; but those here mentioned were at times divinely inspired, and had instructions immediately from heaven upon special occasions, which gave them the title of prophets; and withal they were stated teachers of the church in their religious assemblies, expounded the scriptures, and opened the doctrine of Christ with suitable applications. These were the prophets, and scribes, or teachers, which Christ promised to send (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.34">Matt. xxiii. 34</reference>), such as were every way qualified for the service of the Christian church. Antioch was a great city, and the Christians there were many, so that they could not all meet in one place; it was therefore requisite they should have many teachers, to preside in their respective assemblies, and to deliver God's mind to them. Barnabas is first named, probably because he was the eldest, and Saul last, probably because he was the youngest; but afterwards the last became first, and Saul more eminent in the church. Three others are mentioned. (1.) <hi type="italic">Simeon,</hi> or Simon, who for distinction-sake was called <hi type="italic">Niger, Simon the Black,</hi> from the color of his hair; like him that with us was surnamed the Black Prince. (2.) <hi type="italic">Lucius</hi> of Cyrene, who some think (and Dr. Lightfoot inclines to it) was the same with this Luke that wrote the Acts, originally a Cyrenian, and educated in the Cyrenian college or synagogue at Jerusalem, and there first receiving the gospel. (3.) <hi type="italic">Manaen,</hi> a person of some quality, as it should seem, for he was <hi type="italic">brought up with Herod the tetrarch,</hi> either nursed of the same milk, or bred at the same school, or pupil to the same tutor, or rather one that was his constant colleague and companion—that in every part of his education was his comrade and intimate, which gave him a fair prospect of preferment at court, and yet for Christ's sake he quitted all the hopes of it; like Moses, who, <hi type="italic">when he had come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter.</hi> Had he joined in with Herod, with whom he was brought up, he might have had Blastus's place, and have been his chamberlain; but it is better to be fellow-sufferer with a saint than fellow-persecutor with a tetrarch. <div eID="gen29525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29526" type="x-p"/> 2. How well employed they were (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">They ministered to the Lord, and fasted.</hi> Observe, (1.) Diligent faithful teachers do truly minister unto the Lord. Those that instruct Christians serve Christ; they really do him honour, and carry on the interest of his kingdom. Those that minister to the church in praying and preaching (both which are included here), <hi type="italic">minister unto the Lord,</hi> for they are the church's servants for Christ's sake; to him they must have an eye in their ministrations, and from him they shall have their recompence. (2.) Ministering to the Lord, in one way or other, ought to be the stated business of churches and their teachers; to this work time ought to be set apart, nay, it is set apart, and in this work we ought to spend some part of every day. What have we to do as Christians and ministers but to <hi type="italic">serve the Lord Christ?</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.24">Col. iii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.18">Rom. xiv. 18</reference>. (3.) Religious <hi type="italic">fasting</hi> is of use in our ministering to the Lord, both as a sign of our humiliation and a means of our mortification. Though it was not so much practised by the disciples of Christ, <hi type="italic">while the bridegroom was with them,</hi> as it was by the disciples of John and of the Pharisees; yet, after the bridegroom was taken away, they abounded in it, as those that had well learned to deny themselves and to endure hardness. <div eID="gen29526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29527" type="x-p"/> II. The orders given by the Holy Ghost for the setting apart of Barnabas and Saul, while they were engaged in public exercises, the ministers of the several congregations in the city joining in one solemn fast or day of prayer: The <hi type="italic">Holy Ghost said,</hi> either by a voice from heaven, or by a strong impulse on the minds of those of them that were prophets, <hi type="italic">Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.</hi> He does not specify the work, but refers to a former call of which they themselves knew the meaning, whether others did or no: as for Saul, he was particularly told that he must <hi type="italic">bear Christ's name to the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.15">ch. ix. 15</reference>), that <hi type="italic">he must be sent to the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.21">ch. xxii. 21</reference>); the matter was settled between them at Jerusalem before this, that as Peter, James, and John laid out themselves among those of the circumcision, so Paul and Barnabas should <hi type="italic">go to the heathen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.2.7-Gal.2.9">Gal. ii. 7-9</reference>. Barnabas, it is likely, knew himself designed for this service as well as Paul. Yet they would not thrust themselves into this harvest, though it appeared plenteous, till they received their orders from the Lord of the harvest: <hi type="italic">Thrust in thy sickle for the harvest is ripe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Rev. xiv. 15</reference>. The orders were, <hi type="italic">Separate me Barnabas and Saul.</hi> Observe here, 1. Christ by his Spirit has the nomination of his ministers; for it is by the Spirit of Christ that they are qualified in some measure for his services, inclined to it, and taken off from other cares inconsistent with it. There are some whom the Holy Ghost has separated for the service of Christ, has distinguished from others as men that are offered and that willingly offer themselves to the temple service; and concerning them directions are given to those who are competent judges of the sufficiency of the abilities and the sincerity of the inclination: <hi type="italic">Separate</hi> them. 2. Christ's ministers are separated to him and to the Holy Ghost: <hi type="italic">Separate them to me;</hi> they are to be employed in Christ's work and under the Spirit's guidance, to the glory of God the Father. 3. All that are separated to Christ as his ministers are separated to work; Christ keeps no servants to be idle. <hi type="italic">If any man desires the office of a bishop, he desires a good work;</hi> that is what he is separated to, <hi type="italic">to labour in the word and doctrine.</hi> They are separated to take pains, not to take state. 4. The work of Christ's ministers, to which they are to be separated, is work that is already settled, and that which all Christ's ministers hitherto have been called to, and which they themselves have first been, by an external call, directed to and have chosen. <div eID="gen29527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29528" type="x-p"/> III. Their ordination, pursuant to these orders: not to the ministry in general (Barnabas and Saul had both of them been ministers long before this), but to a particular service in the ministry, which had something peculiar in it, and which required a fresh commission, which commission God saw fit at this time to transmit by the hands of <hi type="italic">these prophets and teachers,</hi> for the giving of this direction to the church, that teachers should ordain teachers (for prophets we are not now any longer to expect), and that those who have the dispensing of the oracles of Christ committed to them should, for the benefit of posterity, <hi type="italic">commit the same to faithful men, who shall be able also to teach others,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">2 Tim. ii. 2</reference>. So here, Simeon, and Lucius, and Manaen, faithful teachers at this time in the church of Antioch, <hi type="italic">when they had fasted and prayed, laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul, and sent them away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">v. 3</reference>), according to the directions received. Observe, 1. They prayed for them. When good men are going forth about good work, they ought to be solemnly and particularly prayed for, especially by their brethren that are their fellow-labourers and fellow-soldiers. 2. They joined fasting with their prayers, as they did in their other ministrations, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">v. 3</reference>. Christ has taught us this by his abstaining from sleep (a night-fast, if I may so call it) the night before he sent forth his apostles, that he might spend it in prayer. 3. They laid their hands on them. Hereby, (1.) They gave them their manumission, dismission, or discharge from the present service they were engaged in, in the church of Antioch, acknowledging that they went off not only fairly and with consent, but honourably and with a good report. (2.) They implored a blessing upon them in their present undertaking, begged that God would be with them, and give them success; and, in order to this, that <hi type="italic">they might be filled with the Holy Ghost</hi> in their work. This very thing is explained <reference osisRef="Acts.14.26">ch. xiv. 26</reference>, where it is said, concerning Paul and Barnabas, that from <hi type="italic">Antioch they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled.</hi> As it was an instance of the humility of Barnabas and Saul that they submitted to the imposition of the hands of those that were their equals, or rather their inferiors; so it was of the good disposition of the other teachers that they did not envy Barnabas and Saul the honour to which they were preferred, but cheerfully committed it to them, with hearty prayers for them; and <hi type="italic">they sent them away</hi> with all expedition, out of a concern for those countries where they were to break up fallow ground.
entries.bdd99fa202a3e972f5e568f473a6a287542e9055: <div eID="gen29528" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Elymas Struck with Blindness.</title> <div sID="gen29529" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> So they, being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, departed unto Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus. 5 And when they were at Salamis, they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews: and they had also John to <hi type="italic">their</hi> minister. <hi type="super">6</hi> And when they had gone through the isle unto Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Bar-jesus: <hi type="super">7</hi> Which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God. <hi type="super">8</hi> But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith. 9 Then Saul, (who also <hi type="italic">is called</hi> Paul,) filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him, <hi type="super">10</hi> And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> child of the devil, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? <hi type="super">11</hi> And now, behold, the hand of the Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord. <hi type="super">13</hi> Now when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia: and John departing from them returned to Jerusalem. <div eID="gen29529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29530" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen29530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29531" type="x-p"/> I. A general account of the coming of Barnabas and Saul to the famous island of Cyprus; and perhaps thitherward they steered their course because Barnabas was a native of that country (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.36">ch. iv. 36</reference>), and he was willing they should have the first-fruits of his labours, pursuant to his new commission. Observe, 1. Their being sent forth by the Holy Ghost was the great thing that encouraged them in this undertaking, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.4">v. 4</reference>. If the Holy Ghost send them forth, he will go along with them, strengthen them, carry them on in their work, and give them success; and then they fear no colours, but can cheerfully venture upon a stormy sea from Antioch, which was now to them a quiet harbour. 2. They came to Seleucia, the sea-port town opposite to Cyprus, thence crossed the sea to Cyprus, and in that island the first city they came to was Salamis, a city on the east side of the island (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.5">v. 5</reference>); and, when they had sown good seed there, <hi type="italic">thence they</hi> went onward <hi type="italic">through the isle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.6">v. 6</reference>) till they came to Paphos, which lay on the western coast. 3. <hi type="italic">They preached the word of God</hi> wherever they came, <hi type="italic">in the synagogues of the Jews;</hi> so far were they from excluding them that they gave them the preference, and so left those among them who believed not inexcusable; <hi type="italic">they would have gathered them, but they would not.</hi> They did not act clandestinely, nor preach the Messiah to others unknown to them, but laid their doctrine open to the censure of the rulers of their synagogues, who might, if they had any thing to say, object against it. Nor would they have acted separately, but in concert with them, if they had not driven them out from them, and from their synagogues. 4. <hi type="italic">They had John for their minister;</hi> not their servant in common things, but their assistant in the things of God, either to prepare their way in places where they designed to come or to carry on their work in places where they had begun it, or to converse familiarly with those to whom they preached publicly, and explain things to them; and such a one might be many ways of use to them, especially in a strange country. <div eID="gen29531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29532" type="x-p"/> II. A particular account of their encounter with <hi type="italic">Elymas the sorcerer,</hi> whom they met with at Paphos, where the governor resided; a place famous for a temple built to Venus there, thence called <hi type="italic">Paphian Venus;</hi> and therefore there was more than ordinary need that <hi type="italic">the Son of God</hi> should there <hi type="italic">be manifested to destroy the works of the devil.</hi> <div eID="gen29532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29533" type="x-p"/> 1. There the <hi type="italic">deputy,</hi> a Gentile, <hi type="italic">Sergius Paulus</hi> by name, encouraged the apostles, and was willing to hear their message. He was governor <hi type="italic">of the country,</hi> under the Roman emperor; proconsul or proprætor, such a one as we should call <hi type="italic">lord lieutenant of the island.</hi> He had the character of <hi type="italic">a prudent man,</hi> an intelligent, considerate man, that was ruled by reason, not passion nor prejudice, which appeared by this, that, having a character of Barnabas and Saul, he sent for them, <hi type="italic">and desired to hear the word of God.</hi> Note, When that which we hear has a tendency to lead us to God, it is prudence to desire to hear more of it. Those are wise people, however they may be ranked among the foolish of this world, who are inquisitive after the mind and will of God. Though he was a great man, and a man in authority, and the preachers of the gospel were men that made no figure, yet, if they have a message from God, let him know what it is, and, if it appear to be so, he is ready to receive it. <div eID="gen29533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29534" type="x-p"/> 2. There Elymas, a Jew, a <hi type="italic">sorcerer,</hi> opposed them, and did all he could to obstruct their progress. This justified the apostles in <hi type="italic">turning to the Gentiles,</hi> that this Jew was so malignant against them. <div eID="gen29534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29535" type="x-p"/> (1.) This Elymas was a pretender <hi type="italic">to the gift of prophecy, a sorcerer, a false-prophet</hi>—one that would be taken for a divine, because he was skilled in the arts of divination; he was a conjurer, and took on him to tell people their fortune, and to discover things lost, and probably was in league with the devil for this purpose; <hi type="italic">his name was Bar-jesus—the son of Joshua;</hi> it signifies <hi type="italic">the son of salvation;</hi> but the Syriac calls him, <hi type="italic">Bar-shoma—the son of pride; filius inflationis—the son of inflation.</hi> <div eID="gen29535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29536" type="x-p"/> (2.) He was hanging on at court, <hi type="italic">was with the deputy</hi> of the country. It does not appear that the deputy called for him, as he did for Barnabas and Saul; but he thrust himself upon him, aiming, no doubt, to make a hand of him, and get money by him. <div eID="gen29536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29537" type="x-p"/> (3.) He made it his business to withstand Barnabas and Saul, as the magicians of Egypt, in Pharaoh's court, <hi type="italic">withstood</hi> Moses and Aaron, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">2 Tim. iii. 8</reference>. He set up himself to be a messenger from heaven, and denied that they were. And <hi type="italic">thus he sought to turn away the deputy from the faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.8">v. 8</reference>), to keep him from receiving the gospel, which he saw him inclined to do. Note, Satan is in a special manner busy with great men and men of power, to keep them from being religious; because he knows that their example, whether good or bad, will have an influence upon many. And those who are in any way instrumental to prejudice people against the truths and ways of Christ are doing the devil's work. <div eID="gen29537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29538" type="x-p"/> (4.) Saul (who is here for the first time called Paul) fell upon him for this with a holy indignation. <hi type="italic">Saul, who is also called Paul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.9">v. 9</reference>. Saul was his name as he was a Hebrew, and of the tribe of Benjamin; Paul was his name as he was a citizen of Rome. Hitherto we have had him mostly conversant among the Jews, and therefore called by his Jewish name; but now, when he is sent forth among the Gentiles, he is called by his Roman name, to put somewhat of a reputation upon him in the Roman cities, Paulus being a very common name among them. But some think he was never called Paul till now that he was instrumental in the conversion of Sergius Paulus to the faith of Christ, and that he took the name Paulus as a memorial of this victory obtained by the gospel of Christ, as among the Romans he that had conquered a country took his denomination from it, as <hi type="italic">Germanicus, Britannicus, Africanus;</hi> or rather, Sergius Paulus himself gave him the name Paulus in token of his favour and respect to him, as Vespasian gave his name Flavius to Josephus the Jew. Now of Paul it is said, <div eID="gen29538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29539" type="x-p"/> [1.] That he was <hi type="italic">filled with the Holy Ghost</hi> upon this occasion, filled with a holy zeal against a professed enemy of Christ, which was one of the graces of the Holy Ghost—<hi type="italic">a spirit of burning;</hi> filled with power to denounce the wrath of God against him, which was one of the gifts of the Holy Ghost—<hi type="italic">a spirit of judgment.</hi> He felt a more than ordinary fervour in his mind, as the prophet did when he was <hi type="italic">full of power by the Spirit of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.8">Mic. iii. 8</reference>), and another prophet when <hi type="italic">his face was made harder than flint</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.9">Ezek. iii. 9</reference>), and another when his <hi type="italic">mouth was made like a sharp sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>. What Paul said did not come from any personal resentment, but from the strong impressions which the Holy Ghost made upon his spirit. <div eID="gen29539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29540" type="x-p"/> [2.] He <hi type="italic">set his eyes upon him,</hi> to face him down, and to show a holy boldness, in opposition to his wicked impudence. He set his eyes upon him, as an indication that the eye of the heart-searching God was upon him, and saw through and through him; nay, <hi type="italic">that the face of the Lord was against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">Ps. xxxiv. 16</reference>. He fixed his eyes upon him, to see if he could discern in his countenance any marks of remorse for what he had done; for, if he could have discerned the least sign of this, it would have prevented the ensuing doom. <div eID="gen29540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29541" type="x-p"/> [3.] He gave him his true character, not in passion, but by the Holy Ghost, who knows men better than they know themselves, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.10">v. 10</reference>. He describes him to be, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> An agent for hell; and such there have been upon this earth (the seat of the war between <hi type="italic">the seed of the woman and of the serpent</hi>) ever since Cain <hi type="italic">who was of that wicked one,</hi> an incarnate devil, <hi type="italic">slew his brother,</hi> for no other reason than because <hi type="italic">his own works were evil and his brother's righteous.</hi> This Elymas, though called <hi type="italic">Bar-jesus—a son of Jesus,</hi> was really a <hi type="italic">child of the devil,</hi> bore his image, did his lusts, and served his interests, <reference osisRef="John.8.44">John viii. 44</reference>. In two things he resembled the devil as a child does his father—1. In craftiness. <hi type="italic">The serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.1">Gen. iii. 1</reference>), and Elymas, though void of all wisdom, was <hi type="italic">full of all subtlety,</hi> expert in all the arts of deceiving men and imposing upon them. 2. In malice. He was <hi type="italic">full of all mischief</hi>—a spiteful ill-conditioned man, and a sworn implacable enemy to God and goodness. Note, A fulness of subtlety and mischief together make a man indeed a child of the devil. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> An adversary to heaven. If he be a child of the devil, it follows of course that he is <hi type="italic">an enemy to all righteousness,</hi> for the devil is so. Note, Those that are enemies to the doctrine of Christ are enemies to all righteousness, for in it all righteousness is summed up and fulfilled. <div eID="gen29541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29542" type="x-p"/> [4.] He charged upon him his present crime, and expostulated with him upon it: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord,</hi> to misrepresent them, to put false colours upon them, and so to discourage people from entering into them, and walking in them?" Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The ways of the Lord are right: they are all so, they are perfectly so. The ways of the Lord Jesus are right, the only right ways to heaven and happiness. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> There are those who pervert these right ways, who not only wander out of these ways themselves (as Elihu's penitent, who owns, <hi type="italic">I have perverted that which was right and it profited me not</hi>), but mislead others, and suggest to them unjust prejudices against these ways: as if the doctrine of Christ were uncertain and precarious, the laws of Christ unreasonable and impractical, and the service of Christ unpleasant and unprofitable, which is an unjust perverting of the right ways of the Lord, and making them seem crooked ways. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Those who pervert the right ways of the Lord are commonly so hardened in it that, though the equity of those ways be set before them by the most powerful and commanding evidence, yet they will not cease to do it. <hi type="italic">Etsi suaseris, non persuaseris—You may advise, but you will never persuade;</hi> they will have it their own way; <hi type="italic">they have loved strangers, and after them they will go.</hi> <div eID="gen29542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29543" type="x-p"/> [5.] He denounced the judgment of God upon him, in a present blindness (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee,</hi> a righteous hand. God is now about to lay hands on thee, and make thee his prisoner, for thou art taken in arms against him; <hi type="italic">thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season.</hi>" This was designed both for the proof of his crime, as it was a miracle wrought to confirm the right ways of the Lord, and consequently to show the wickedness of him who would not cease to pervert them, as also for the punishment of his crime. It was a suitable punishment; he shut his eyes, the eyes of his mind, against the light of the gospel, and therefore justly were the eyes of his body shut against the light of the sun; he sought to blind the deputy (as an agent for <hi type="italic">the god of this world, who blindeth the minds of those that believe not, lest the light of the gospel should shine unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2 Cor. iv. 4</reference>), and therefore is himself struck blind. Yet it was a moderate punishment: he was only struck blind, when he might most justly have been struck dead; and it was only <hi type="italic">for a season;</hi> if he will repent, and give glory to God, by making confession, his sight shall be restored; nay, it should seem, though he do not, yet his sight shall be restored, to try if he will be led to repentance either by the judgments of God or by his mercies. <div eID="gen29543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29544" type="x-p"/> [6.] This judgment was immediately executed: <hi type="italic">There fell on him a mist and a darkness,</hi> as on the Sodomites when they persecuted Elisha. This silenced him presently, filled him with confusion, and was an effectual confutation of all he said against the doctrine of Christ. Let not him any more pretend to be a guide to the deputy's conscience who is himself struck blind. It was also an earnest to him of a much sorer punishment if he repent not; for he is one of those <hi type="italic">wandering stars to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.13">Jude 13</reference>. Elymas did himself proclaim the truth of the miracle, when <hi type="italic">he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand;</hi> and where now is all his skill in sorcery, upon which he had so much valued himself, when he can neither find his way nor find a friend that will be so kind as to lead him! <div eID="gen29544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29545" type="x-p"/> 3. Notwithstanding all the endeavours of Elymas <hi type="italic">to turn away the deputy from the faith,</hi> he was brought to believe, and this miracle, wrought upon the magician himself (like <hi type="italic">the boils of Egypt,</hi> which <hi type="italic">were upon the magicians, so that they could not stand before Moses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.9.11">Exod. ix. 11</reference>), contributed to it. The deputy was a very sensible man, and observed something uncommon, and which intimated its divine original, (1.) In Paul's preaching: he was <hi type="italic">astonished at the doctrine of the Lord,</hi> the Lord Christ—the doctrine that <hi type="italic">is from him,</hi> the discoveries he has made of the Father—the doctrine that <hi type="italic">is concerning him,</hi> his person, natures, offices, undertaking. Note, The doctrine of Christ has a great deal in it that is astonishing; and the more we know of it the more reason we shall see to wonder and stand amazed at it. (2.) In this miracle: <hi type="italic">When he saw what was done,</hi> and how much Paul's power transcended that of the magician, and how plainly Elymas was baffled and confounded, he believed. It is not said that he was baptized, and so made a complete convert, but it is probable that he was. Paul would not do his business by the halves; <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect.</hi> When he became a Christian, he neither laid down his government, nor was turned out of it, but we may suppose, as a Christian magistrate, by his influence helped very much to propagate Christianity in that island. The tradition of the Romish church, which has taken care to find bishoprics for all the eminent converts we read of in <hi type="italic">the Acts,</hi> has made this Sergius Paulus bishop of Narbon in France, left there by Paul in his journey to Spain. <div eID="gen29545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29546" type="x-p"/> III. Their departure from the island of Cyprus. It is probable that they did a great deal more there than is recorded, where an account is given only of that which was extraordinary—the conversion of the deputy. When they had done what they had to do, 1. They quitted the country, and <hi type="italic">went to Perga.</hi> Those that went were <hi type="italic">Paul and his company,</hi> which, it is probable, was increased in Cyprus, many being desirous to accompany him. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Anachthentes hoi peri ton Paulon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Those that were about Paul loosed from Paphos,</hi> which supposes that he went too; but such an affection had his new friends for him that they were always about him, and by their good will would be never from him. 2. Then John <hi type="italic">Mark quitted them, and returned to Jerusalem,</hi> without the consent of Paul and Barnabas; either he did not like the work, or he wanted to go and see his mother. It was his fault, and we shall hear of it again.
entries.17b1e95e4bd69d7a092e7ace5fba14f5c882495b: <div eID="gen29546" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul at Antioch in Pisidia.</title> <div sID="gen29547" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> But when they departed from Perga, they came to Antioch in Pisidia, and went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and sat down. <hi type="super">15</hi> And after the reading of the law and the prophets the rulers of the synagogue sent unto them, saying, <hi type="italic">Ye</hi> men <hi type="italic">and</hi> brethren, if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then Paul stood up, and beckoning with <hi type="italic">his</hi> hand said, Men of Israel, and ye that fear God, give audience. <hi type="super">17</hi> The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt, and with a high arm brought he them out of it. <hi type="super">18</hi> And about the time of forty years suffered he their manners in the wilderness. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Chanaan, he divided their land to them by lot. <hi type="super">20</hi> And after that he gave <hi type="italic">unto them</hi> judges about the space of four hundred and fifty years, until Samuel the prophet. <hi type="super">21</hi> And afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of forty years. <hi type="super">22</hi> And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will. <hi type="super">23</hi> Of this man's seed hath God according to <hi type="italic">his</hi> promise raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus: <hi type="super">24</hi> When John had first preached before his coming the baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. <hi type="super">25</hi> And as John fulfilled his course, he said, Whom think ye that I am? I am not <hi type="italic">he.</hi> But, behold, there cometh one after me, whose shoes of <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet I am not worthy to loose. <hi type="super">26</hi> Men <hi type="italic">and</hi> brethren, children of the stock of Abraham, and whosoever among you feareth God, to you is the word of this salvation sent. <hi type="super">27</hi> For they that dwell at Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they knew him not, nor yet the voices of the prophets which are read every sabbath day, they have fulfilled <hi type="italic">them</hi> in condemning <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">28</hi> And though they found no cause of death <hi type="italic">in him,</hi> yet desired they Pilate that he should be slain. <hi type="super">29</hi> And when they had fulfilled all that was written of him, they took <hi type="italic">him</hi> down from the tree, and laid <hi type="italic">him</hi> in a sepulchre. 30 But God raised him from the dead: <hi type="super">31</hi> And he was seen many days of them which came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses unto the people. <hi type="super">32</hi> And we declare unto you glad tidings, how that the promise which was made unto the fathers, <hi type="super">33</hi> God hath fulfilled the same unto us their children, in that he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. <hi type="super">34</hi> And as concerning that he raised him up from the dead, <hi type="italic">now</hi> no more to return to corruption, he said on this wise, I will give you the sure mercies of David. <hi type="super">35</hi> Wherefore he saith also in another <hi type="italic">psalm,</hi> Thou shalt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. <hi type="super">36</hi> For David, after he had served his own generation by the will of God, fell on sleep, and was laid unto his fathers, and saw corruption: <hi type="super">37</hi> But he, whom God raised again, saw no corruption. <hi type="super">38</hi> Be it known unto you therefore, men <hi type="italic">and</hi> brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: <hi type="super">39</hi> And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses. <hi type="super">40</hi> Beware therefore, lest that come upon you, which is spoken of in the prophets; <hi type="super">41</hi> Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you. <div eID="gen29547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29548" type="x-p"/> Perga in Pamphylia was a noted place, especially for a temple there erected to the goddess Diana, yet nothing at all is related of what Paul and Barnabas did there, only that <hi type="italic">thither they came</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.13">v. 13</reference>), and <hi type="italic">thence they departed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.14">v. 14</reference>. But the history of the apostles' travels, as that of Christ's, passes by many things worthy to have been recorded, because, <hi type="italic">if all had been written, the world could not have contained the books.</hi> But the next place we find them in is another Antioch, said to be in Pisidia, to distinguish it from that Antioch in Syria from which they were sent out. Pisidia was a province of the Lesser Asia, bordering upon Pamphylia; this Antioch, it is likely, was the metropolis of it. Abundance of Jews lived there, and to them <hi type="italic">the gospel was to be first preached;</hi> and Paul's sermon to them is what we have in these verses, which, it is likely, is the substance of what was preached by the apostles generally to the Jews in all places; for in dealing with them the proper way was to show them how the New Testament, which they would have them to receive, exactly agreed with the Old Testament, which they not only received, but were zealous for. We have here, <div eID="gen29548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29549" type="x-p"/> I. The appearance which Paul and Barnabas made in a religious assembly of the Jews at Antioch, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.14">v. 14</reference>. Though they had lately had such good success with a Roman deputy, yet, <hi type="italic">when they came to Antioch,</hi> they did not enquire for the chief magistrate, nor make their court to him, but they applied to the Jews, which is a further proof of their good affection to them and their desire of their welfare. 1. They observed their time of worship, <hi type="italic">on the sabbath day,</hi> the Jewish sabbath. <hi type="italic">The first day of the week</hi> they observed among themselves as a Christian sabbath; but, if they will meet the Jews, it must be on the seventh-day sabbath, which therefore, upon such occasions, they did as yet sometimes observe. For, though it was by the death of Christ that the ceremonial law died, yet it was in the ruins of Jerusalem that it was to be buried; and therefore, though the morality of the fourth commandment was entirely transferred to the Christian sabbath, yet it was not incongruous to join with the Jews in their sabbath sanctification. 2. They met them in their place of worship, <hi type="italic">in the synagogue.</hi> Note, Sabbath days should be kept holy in solemn assemblies; they are instituted chiefly for public worship. <hi type="italic">The sabbath day is a holy convocation,</hi> and for that reason <hi type="italic">no servile work must be done therein.</hi> Paul and Barnabas were strangers; but, wherever we come, we must enquire out God's faithful worshippers, and join with them (as these apostles here did), as those that desire to keep up a communion with all saints; though they were strangers, yet they were admitted into the synagogue, and to sit down there. Care should be taken in places of public worship that strangers be accommodated, even the poorest; for, of those of whom we know nothing else, we know this, that they have precious souls, for which our charity binds us to be concerned. <div eID="gen29549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29550" type="x-p"/> II. The invitation given them to preach. 1. The usual service of the synagogue was performed (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">The law and the prophets were read,</hi> a portion of each, the lessons for the day. Note, When we come together to worship God, we must do it not only by prayer and praise, but by the reading and hearing of the word of God; hereby we <hi type="italic">give him the glory due to his name,</hi> as our Lord and Lawgiver. 2. When that was done, they were asked by <hi type="italic">the rulers of the synagogue</hi> to give them a sermon (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.15">v. 15</reference>): They sent a messenger to them with the respectful message, <hi type="italic">Men and brethren, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, say on.</hi> It is probable that the rulers of the synagogue had met with them, and been in private conversation with them before; and, if they had not an affection to the gospel, yet they had at least the curiosity to hear Paul preach; and therefore not only gave him permission, but begged the favour of him that he would speak a <hi type="italic">word of exhortation to the people.</hi> Note, (1.) The bare reading of the scriptures in the public assemblies is not sufficient, but they should be expounded, and the people exhorted out of them. This is spreading the net, and assisting people in doing that which is necessary to the making of the word profitable to them—that is, the applying of it to themselves. (2.) Those that preside, and have power, in public assemblies, should provide for a word of exhortation to the people, whenever they come together. (3.) Sometimes a word of exhortation from a strange minister may be of great use to the people, provided he be well approved. It is likely Paul did <hi type="italic">often preach in the synagogue,</hi> when he was not thus invited to it by the rulers of the synagogues; for he often preached <hi type="italic">with much contention,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1 Thess. ii. 2</reference>. But these were more noble, more generous, than the rulers of the synagogues generally were. <div eID="gen29550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29551" type="x-p"/> III. The sermon Paul preached in the synagogue of the Jews, at the invitation of the rulers of the synagogue. He gladly embraced the opportunity given him to preach Christ to his countrymen the Jews. He did not object to them that he was a stranger, and that it was none of his business; nor object to himself, that he might get ill-will by preaching Christ among the Jews; but <hi type="italic">stood up,</hi> as one prepared and determined to speak, <hi type="italic">and beckoned with his hand,</hi> to excite and prepare them to hear. He waved his hand as an orator, not only desiring silence and attention, but endeavouring to move affection, and to show himself in earnest. Perhaps, upon the moving of them <hi type="italic">to give an exhortation to the people,</hi> there were those in the synagogue that were ready to mutiny against the rulers, and opposed the toleration of Paul's preaching, and that occasioned some tumult and commotion, which Paul endeavoured to quiet by that decent motion of his hand; as also by his modest desire of a patient impartial hearing: "<hi type="italic">Men of Israel,</hi> that are <hi type="italic">Jews</hi> by birth, <hi type="italic">and you that fear God,</hi> that are proselyted to the Jewish religion, <hi type="italic">give audience;</hi> let me beg your attention a little, for I have something to say to you which concerns your everlasting peace, and would not say it in vain." Now this excellent sermon is recorded, to show that those who preached the gospel to the Gentiles did it not till they had first used their utmost endeavours with the Jews, to persuade them to come in and take the benefit of it; and that they had no prejudice at all against the Jewish nation, nor any desire <hi type="italic">that they should perish, but rather that they should turn and live.</hi> Every thing is touched in this sermon that might be proper either to convince the judgment or insinuate into the affections of the Jews, to prevail with them to receive and embrace Christ as the promised Messiah. <div eID="gen29551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29552" type="x-p"/> 1. He owns them to be God's favourite people, whom he had taken into special relation to himself, and for whom he had done great things. Probably <hi type="italic">the Jews of the dispersion,</hi> that lived in other countries, being more in danger of mingling with the nations, were more jealous of their peculiarity than those that lived in their own land were; and therefore Paul is here very careful to take notice of it, to their honour. <div eID="gen29552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29553" type="x-p"/> (1.) That <hi type="italic">the God of the whole earth</hi> was, in a particular manner, <hi type="italic">the God of this people Israel,</hi> a God <hi type="italic">in covenant with them,</hi> and that he had given them a revelation of his mind and will, such as he <hi type="italic">had not given to any other nation or people;</hi> so that hereby they were distinguished from, and dignified above, all their neighbours, having peculiar precepts to be governed by, and peculiar promises to depend upon. <div eID="gen29553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29554" type="x-p"/> (2.) That he had <hi type="italic">chosen their fathers</hi> to be his friends: Abraham was called <hi type="italic">the friend of God;</hi> to be his prophets, by whom he would reveal his mind to his church, and to be the trustees of his covenant with the church. He puts them in mind of this, to let them know that the reason why God favoured them, though undeserving, and ill deserving, was because he would adhere to the choice he had made of <hi type="italic">their fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.7.7-Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">They were beloved</hi> purely <hi type="italic">for the fathers' sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen29554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29555" type="x-p"/> (3.) That he had <hi type="italic">exalted that people,</hi> and put a great deal of honour upon them, had advanced them into a people, and raised them from nothing, <hi type="italic">when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt,</hi> and had nothing in them to recommend them to the divine favour. They ought to remember this, and to infer hence that God was no debtor to them; for it was <hi type="italic">ex mero motu—out of his mere good pleasure,</hi> and not upon a valuable consideration, that they had the grant of the divine favour; and therefore it was revocable at pleasure; and God did them no wrong if he at length plucked up the hedge of their peculiarity. But they were debtors to him, and obliged to receive such further discoveries as he should make to his church. <div eID="gen29555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29556" type="x-p"/> (4.) That he had <hi type="italic">with a high hand brought them out of Egypt,</hi> where they were not only strangers, but captives, had delivered them at the expense of a great many miracles, both of mercy to them and judgment on their oppressors (<hi type="italic">signs and wonders,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deut. iv. 34</reference>), and at the expense of a great many lives, <hi type="italic">all the first-born of Egypt, Pharaoh, and all his host, in the Red Sea; I gave Egypt for thy ransom, gave men for thee.</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3-Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen29556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29557" type="x-p"/> (5.) That <hi type="italic">he had suffered their manners forty years in the wilderness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.18">v. 18</reference>, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Etropophoresen.</hi></hi> Some think it should be read, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">etrophophoresen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he educated them,</hi> because this is the word the Septuagint use concerning the fatherly care God took of that people, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.31">Deut. i. 31</reference>. Both may be included; for, [1.] God made a great deal of provision for them for forty years in the wilderness: miracles were their daily bread, and kept them from starving: <hi type="italic">They lacked not any thing.</hi> [2.] He exercised a great deal of patience with them. They were a provoking, murmuring, unbelieving people; and yet he bore with them, did not deal with them as they deserved, but suffered his anger many a time to be turned away by the prayer and intercession of Moses. So many years as we have each of us lived in this world, we must own that God has thus been as a tender father to us, has supplied our wants, has <hi type="italic">fed us all our life long unto this day,</hi> has been indulgent to us, a God of pardons (as he was to Israel, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.17">Neh. ix. 17</reference>), and <hi type="italic">not extreme to mark what we have done amiss;</hi> we have tried his patience, and yet not tired it. Let not the Jews insist too much upon the privileges of their peculiarity, for they have forfeited them a thousand times. <div eID="gen29557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29558" type="x-p"/> (6.) That he had put them in possession of the land of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan,</hi> that were doomed to be rooted out to make room for them, <hi type="italic">he divided their land to them by lot,</hi> and put them in possession of it. This was a signal favour of God to them, and he owns that hereby a great honour was put upon them, from which he would not in the least derogate. <div eID="gen29558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29559" type="x-p"/> (7.) That he had raised up men, inspirited from heaven, to deliver them out of the hands of those that invaded their rights, and oppressed them after their settlement in Canaan, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.20-Acts.13.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. [1.] He <hi type="italic">gave them judges,</hi> men qualified for public service, and, by an immediate impulse upon their spirits, called to it, <hi type="italic">pro re nata—as the occasion required.</hi> Though they were a provoking people, and were never in servitude but their sin brought them to it, yet upon their petition a deliverer was raised up. The critics find some difficulty in computing <hi type="italic">these four hundred and fifty years.</hi> From the <hi type="italic">deliverance out of Egypt</hi> to David's expulsion of <hi type="italic">the Jebusites from the stronghold of Zion,</hi> which completed the casting out of the heathen nations, <hi type="italic">was four hundred and fifty years;</hi> and most of that time they were under judges. Others thus: The government of the judges, from the death of Joshua to the death of Eli, was just <hi type="italic">three hundred and thirty-nine years,</hi> but it is said to be [<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">os</hi></hi>] as it were <hi type="italic">four hundred and fifty years,</hi> because the years of their servitude to the several nations that oppressed them, though really they were included in the years of the judges, are yet mentioned in the history as if they had been distinct from them. Now these, all put together, make <hi type="italic">one hundred and eleven years,</hi> which added to the <hi type="italic">three hundred and thirty nine,</hi> make them <hi type="italic">four hundred and fifty;</hi> as so many, though not really so many. [2.] He governed them by a <hi type="italic">prophet, Samuel,</hi> a man divinely inspired to preside in their affairs. [3.] He <hi type="italic">afterwards</hi> at their request <hi type="italic">set a king over them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">Saul, the son of Cis.</hi> Samuel's government and his lasted <hi type="italic">forty years,</hi> which was a kind of transition from the theocracy to the kingly government. [4.] At last, he made David their king, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.22">v. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">When God had removed Saul,</hi> for his mal-administration, <hi type="italic">he raised up unto them David to be their king,</hi> and made <hi type="italic">a covenant of royalty with him, and with his seed.</hi> When he had removed one king, he did not leave them as sheep without a shepherd, but soon raised up another, raised him up from a mean and low estate, <hi type="italic">raised him up on high,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">2 Sam. xxiii. 1</reference>. He quotes the testimony God gave concerning him, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That his choice was divine: <hi type="italic">I have found David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.20">Ps. lxxxix. 20</reference>. God himself pitched upon him. Finding implies seeking; as if God had ransacked all the families of Israel to find a man fit for his purpose, and this was he. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That his character was divine: <hi type="italic">A man after my own heart,</hi> such a one as I would have, one on whom the image of God is stamped, and therefore one in whom God is well pleased and whom he approves. This character was given of him before he was first anointed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.14">1 Sam. xiii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord hath sought out a man after his own heart,</hi> such a one as he would have. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That his conduct was divine, and under divine direction: <hi type="italic">He shall fulfil all my will.</hi> He shall desire and endeavour to do the will of God, and shall be enabled to do it, and employed in the doing of it, and go through with it. Now all this seems to show not only the special favour of God to the people of Israel (with the acknowledgment of which the apostle is very willing to oblige them) but the further favours of another nature which he designed them, and which were now, by the preaching of the gospel, offered to them. Their deliverance out of Egypt, and settlement in Canaan, <hi type="italic">were types and figures of good things to come.</hi> The changes of their government showed that it <hi type="italic">made nothing perfect,</hi> and therefore must give way to the spiritual kingdom of the Messiah, which was now in the setting up, and which, if they would admit it and submit to it, would be <hi type="italic">the glory of their people Israel;</hi> and therefore they needed not conceive any jealousy at all of the preaching of the gospel, as if it tended in the least to damage the true excellences of the Jewish church. <div eID="gen29559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29560" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives them a full account of our Lord Jesus, passing from David to the Son of David, and shows that this Jesus is his promised Seed (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Of this man's seed,</hi> from that <hi type="italic">root of Jesse,</hi> from that <hi type="italic">man after God's own heart, hath God, according to his promise, raised unto Israel a Saviour—Jesus,</hi> who carries salvation in his name. <div eID="gen29560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29561" type="x-p"/> (1.) How welcome should the preaching of the gospel of Christ be to the Jews, and how should they embrace it, as <hi type="italic">well worthy of all acceptation,</hi> when it brought them the tidings, [1.] Of a Saviour, to deliver <hi type="italic">them out of the hands of their enemies,</hi> as the judges of old, who were therefore called <hi type="italic">saviours;</hi> but this <hi type="italic">a Saviour</hi> to do that for them which, it appears by the history, those could not do—<hi type="italic">to save them from their sins,</hi> their worst enemies. [2.] A Saviour of God's raising up, that has his commission from heaven. [3.] Raised up <hi type="italic">to be a Saviour unto Israel,</hi> to them in the first place: <hi type="italic">He was sent to bless them;</hi> so far was the gospel from designing the gathering of them. [4.] Raised up <hi type="italic">of the seed of David,</hi> that ancient royal family, which the people of Israel gloried so much in, and which at this time, to the great disgrace of the whole nation, was buried in obscurity. It ought to be a great satisfaction to them <hi type="italic">that God had raised up this horn of salvation for them in the house of his servant David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">Luke i. 69</reference>. [5.] Raised up <hi type="italic">according to his promise,</hi> the promise to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.11">Ps. cxxxii. 11</reference>), the promise to the Old-Testament church in the latter times of it: <hi type="italic">I will raise unto David a righteous branch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer. xxiii. 5</reference>. This promise was it <hi type="italic">to which the twelve tribes hoped to come</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.7">ch. xxvi. 7</reference>); why then should they entertain it so coldly, now that it was brought to them? Now, <div eID="gen29561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29562" type="x-p"/> (2.) Concerning this Jesus, he tells them, <div eID="gen29562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29563" type="x-p"/> [1.] That John the Baptist was his harbinger and forerunner, that great man whom all acknowledged to be a prophet. Let them not say that the Messiah's coming was a surprise upon them, and that this might excuse them if they took time to consider whether they should entertain him or no; for they had sufficient warning by John, who <hi type="italic">preached before his coming,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.24">v. 24</reference>. Two things he did—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> He made way for his entrance, by preaching <hi type="italic">the baptism of repentance,</hi> not to a few select disciples, but <hi type="italic">to all the people of Israel.</hi> He showed them their sins, <hi type="italic">warned them of the wrath to come, called them to repentance,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to bring forth fruits meet for repentance,</hi> and bound those to this who were willing to be bound by the solemn rite or sign of baptism; and by this he <hi type="italic">made ready a people prepared for the Lord Jesus,</hi> to whom his grace would be acceptable when they were thus brought to know themselves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He gave notice of his approach (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">As he fulfilled his course,</hi> when he was going on vigorously in his work, and had had wonderful success in it, and an established interest: "Now," saith he to those that attended his ministry, "<hi type="italic">Whom think you that I am?</hi> What notions have you of me, what expectations from me? You may be thinking that I am <hi type="italic">the Messiah,</hi> whom you expect; but you are mistaken, <hi type="italic">I am not he</hi> (see <reference osisRef="John.1.20">John i. 20</reference>), but he is at the door; <hi type="italic">behold, there cometh one</hi> immediately <hi type="italic">after me,</hi> who will so far exceed me upon all accounts, <hi type="italic">that I am not worthy</hi> to be employed in the meanest office about him, no, not to help him on and off with his shoes—<hi type="italic">whose shoes of his feet I am not worthy to loose,</hi> and you may guess who that must be." <div eID="gen29563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29564" type="x-p"/> [2.] That the rulers and people of the Jews, who should have welcomed him, and been his willing, forward, faithful subjects, were his persecutors and murderers. When the apostles preach Christ as <hi type="italic">the Saviour,</hi> they are so far from concealing his ignominious death, and drawing a veil over it, that they always <hi type="italic">preach Christ crucified,</hi> yea, and (though this added much to the reproach of his sufferings) crucified by his own people, by <hi type="italic">those that dwelt in Jerusalem,</hi> the holy city—the royal city, and <hi type="italic">their rulers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.27">v. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their sin was <hi type="italic">that though they found no cause of death in him,</hi> could not prove him, no, nor had any colour to suspect him, guilty of any crime (the judge himself that tried him, when he had heard all they could say against him, declared he <hi type="italic">found no fault with him), yet they desired Pilate that he might be slain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.28">v. 28</reference>), and presented their address against Christ with such fury and outrage that they compelled Pilate to crucify him, not only contrary to his inclination, but contrary to his conscience; they condemned him <hi type="italic">to so great a death,</hi> though they could not convict him of the least sin. Paul cannot charge this upon his hearers, as Peter did (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">ch. ii. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have with wicked hands crucified and slain him;</hi> for these, though Jews, were far enough off; but he charges it upon the Jews at Jerusalem and the rulers, to show what little reason those Jews of the dispersion had to be so jealous for the honour of their nation as they were, when it had brought upon itself such a load and stain of guilt as this, and how justly they might have been cut off from all benefit by the Messiah, who had thus abused him, and yet they were not; but, notwithstanding all this, the preaching of this gospel shall begin at Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The reason of this was because <hi type="italic">they knew him not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.27">v. 27</reference>. They knew not who he was, nor what errand he came into the world upon; for, <hi type="italic">if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.</hi> Christ owned this in extenuation of their crime: <hi type="italic">They know not what they do;</hi> and so did Peter: <hi type="italic">I wot that through ignorance you did this,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.3.17">ch. iii. 17</reference>. It was also because they knew not the voice of the prophets though they heard them read every sabbath day. They did not understand nor consider that it was foretold that the Messiah should suffer, or else they would never have been the instruments of his suffering. Note, Many that read the prophets do not know the voice of the prophets, do not understand the meaning of the scriptures; they have the sound of the gospel in their ears, but not the sense of it in their heads, nor the savour of it in their hearts. And <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> men do not know Christ, nor know how to carry it towards him, because they do not know the voice of the prophets, who <hi type="italic">testified beforehand concerning Christ. Thirdly,</hi> God overruled them, for the accomplishment of the prophecies of the Old-Testament: <hi type="italic">Because they knew not the voice of the prophets,</hi> which warned them not to touch God's Anointed, <hi type="italic">they fulfilled them in condemning him;</hi> for so it was written that <hi type="italic">Messiah the prince shall be cut off, but not for himself.</hi> Note, It is possible that men may be fulfilling scripture prophecies, even when they are breaking scripture precepts, particularly in the persecution of the church, as in the persecution of Christ. And this justifies the reason which is sometimes given for the obscurity of scripture prophecies, that, if they were too plain and obvious, the accomplishment of them would thereby be prevented. So Paul saith here, <hi type="italic">Because they knew not the voice of the prophets,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">they have fulfilled them,</hi> which implies that if they had understood them they would not have fulfilled them. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> All that was foretold concerning the sufferings of the Messiah was fulfilled in Christ (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">When they had fulfilled all</hi> the rest <hi type="italic">that was written of him,</hi> even to the giving of him vinegar to drink in his thirst, then they fulfilled what was foretold concerning his being buried. They <hi type="italic">took him down from the tree, and laid him in a sepulchre.</hi> This is taken notice of here as that which made his resurrection the more illustrious. Christ was separated from this world, as those that are buried have nothing more to do with this world, nor this world with them; and therefore our complete separation from sin is represented by our being <hi type="italic">buried with Christ.</hi> And a good Christian will be willing to be buried alive with Christ. They laid him in a sepulchre, and thought they had him fast. <div eID="gen29564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29565" type="x-p"/> [3.] That he <hi type="italic">rose again from the dead,</hi> and saw no corruption. This was the great truth that was to be preached; for it is the main pillar, by which the whole fabric of the gospel is supported, and therefore he insists largely upon this, and shows, <div eID="gen29565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29566" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he rose by consent. When he was imprisoned in the grave for our debt, he did not break prison, but had a fair and legal discharge from the arrest he was under (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">God raised him from the dead,</hi> sent an angel on purpose to roll away the stone from the prison-door, returned to him the spirit which at his death he had committed into the hands of his Father, and quickened him by the Holy Ghost. His enemies laid him in a sepulchre, with design he should always lay there; but God said, <hi type="italic">No;</hi> and it was soon seen whose purpose should stand, his or theirs. <div eID="gen29566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29567" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That there was sufficient proof of his having risen (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">He was seen many days,</hi> in divers places, upon divers occasions, by those that were most intimately acquainted with him; for they <hi type="italic">came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem,</hi> were his constant attendants, and <hi type="italic">they are his witnesses unto the people.</hi> They were appointed to be so, have attested the thing many a time, and are ready to attest it, though they were to die for the same. Paul says nothing of his own seeing him, which was more convincing to himself than it could be when produced to others. <div eID="gen29567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29568" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That the resurrection of Christ was the performance of the promise made to the patriarchs; it was not only true news, but good news: "In declaring this, we <hi type="italic">declare unto you glad tidings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.32-Acts.13.33">v. 32, 33</reference>), which should be in a particular manner acceptable to you Jews. So far are we from designing to put any slur upon you, or do you any wrong, that the doctrine we preach, if you receive it aright, and understand it, brings you the greatest honour and satisfaction imaginable; for it is in the resurrection of Christ that <hi type="italic">the promise which was made to your fathers is fulfilled to you.</hi>" He acknowledges it to be the dignity of the Jewish nation that <hi type="italic">to them pertained the promises</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>), that they were the heirs of the promise, as they were the children of the patriarchs to whom the promises were first made. The great promise of the Old Testament was that of the Messiah, <hi type="italic">in whom all the families of the earth should be blessed,</hi> and not the family of Abraham only; though it was to be the peculiar honour of that family that he should be raised up of it, yet it was to be the common benefit of all families that he should be raised up to them. Note, 1. God hath <hi type="italic">raised up Jesus,</hi> advanced him, and exalted him; <hi type="italic">raised</hi> him <hi type="italic">again</hi> (so we read it), meaning <hi type="italic">from the dead.</hi> We may take in both senses. God raised up Jesus to be a prophet at his baptism, to be a priest to make atonement at his death, and to be a king to rule over all at his ascension; and <hi type="italic">his raising him up from the dead</hi> was the confirmation and ratification of all these commissions, and proved him raised of God to these offices. 2. This is the fulfilling of the promises made to the fathers, the promise of sending the Messiah, and of all those benefits and blessings which were to be had with him and by him: "This is he that should come, and in him you have all that God promised in the Messiah, though not all that you promised yourselves." Paul puts himself into the number of the Jews to whom the promise was fulfilled: <hi type="italic">To us their children.</hi> Now, if those who preached the gospel brought them <hi type="italic">these glad tidings,</hi> instead of looking upon them as enemies to their nation, they ought to caress them as their best friends, and embrace their doctrine with both arms; for if they valued the promise so much, and themselves by it, much more the performance. And the preaching of the gospel to the Gentiles, which was the great thing that the Jews found themselves aggrieved at, was so far from infringing the promise made to them that the promise itself, that <hi type="italic">all the families of the earth</hi> should be blessed in the Messiah, could not otherwise be accomplished. <div eID="gen29568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29569" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That the resurrection of Christ was the great proof of his being the Son of God, and confirms what was written in the second Psalm (thus ancient was the order in which the Psalms are now placed), <hi type="italic">Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee.</hi> That the resurrection of Christ from the dead was designed to evidence and evince this is plain from that of the apostle (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Rom. i. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He was declared to be the Son of God with power, by the resurrection from the dead.</hi> When he was first raised up out of obscurity, God declared concerning him by a voice from heaven, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>), which has a plain reference to that in the second Psalm, <hi type="italic">Thou art my Son.</hi> Abundance of truth there is couched in those words: that this Jesus was <hi type="italic">begotten of the Father before all worlds</hi>—was <hi type="italic">the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person,</hi> as the son is of the father's—that he was the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">logos,</hi></hi> the <hi type="italic">eternal thought of the eternal mind,</hi>—that he was conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the virgin; for upon this account, also, <hi type="italic">that holy thing was called the Son of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.35">Luke i. 35</reference>), that he was God's agent in creating and governing the world, and in redeeming it and reconciling it to himself, and <hi type="italic">faithful as a son in his own house,</hi> and as such was <hi type="italic">heir of all things.</hi> Now all this, which was declared at Christ's baptism and again at his transfiguration, was undeniably proved by his resurrection. The decree which was so long before declared was then confirmed; and the reason why it was impossible he should be held by the bands of death was because he was the Son of God, and consequently had <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> which he could not lay down but with a design to resume it. When his eternal generation is spoken of, it is not improper to say, <hi type="italic">This day have I begotten thee;</hi> for <hi type="italic">from everlasting to everlasting</hi> is with God as it were one and the same eternal day. Yet it may also be accommodated to his resurrection, in a subordinate sense, "This day have I made it to appear that I have begotten thee, and this day have I begotten all that are given to thee;" for it is said (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1 Pet. i. 3</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> as our God and Father, <hi type="italic">hath begotten us again to a lively hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen29569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29570" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> That his being raised the third day, so as not to see corruption, and to a heavenly life, so as no more to return to corruption, that is, to the state of the dead, as others did who were raised to life, further confirms his being the Messiah promised. <div eID="gen29570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29571" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> He rose to die no more; so it is expressed, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.9">Rom. vi. 9</reference>: <hi type="italic">As concerning that he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption,</hi> that is, to the grave, which is called <hi type="italic">corruption,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.17.14">Job xvii. 14</reference>. Lazarus came out of the grave with his grave-clothes on, because he was to use them again; but Christ, having no more occasion for them, left them behind. Now this was the fulfilling of that scripture (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will give you the sure mercies of David;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta hosia Dabid ta pista</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the holy things of David, the faithful things;</hi> for in the promise made to David, and in him to Christ, great stress is laid upon the faithfulness of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.1-Ps.89.2 Ps.89.5 Ps.89.24 Ps.89.33">Ps. lxxxix. 1, 2, 5, 24, 33</reference>), and upon the oath God had sworn <hi type="italic">by his holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Ps. lxxxix. 35</reference>. Now this makes them sure mercies indeed that he who is entrusted with the dispensing of them has risen to die no more; so that he ever lives to see his own will executed, and the blessings he hath purchased for us given out to us. As, if Christ had died and had not risen again, so if he had risen to die again, we had come short of the sure mercies, or at least could not have been sure of them. <div eID="gen29571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29572" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> He rose so soon after he was dead that his body did not see corruption; for it is not till the third day that the body begins to change. Now this was promised to David; it was one of <hi type="italic">the sure mercies of David,</hi> for it was said to him in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Ps. xvi. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Neither wilt thou suffer thy Holy One to see corruption,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.35">v. 35</reference>. God had promised to David that he would raise up the Messiah of his seed, who should therefore be a man, but should not, like other men, see corruption. This promise could not have its accomplishment in David, but looked forward to Christ. <div eID="gen29572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29573" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) It could not be accomplished in David himself (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">v. 36</reference>), for <hi type="italic">David, after he had served his own generation, by the will of God,</hi> who raised him up to be what he was, <hi type="italic">fell asleep, and was laid to his fathers, and saw corruption.</hi> Here we have a short account of the life, death, and burial, of the patriarch David, and his continuance under the power of death. [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] His life: <hi type="italic">He served his own generation, by the will of God,</hi> before he slept the sleep of death. David was a useful good man; he did good in the world <hi type="italic">by the will of God.</hi> He made God's precepts his rule; he <hi type="italic">served his own generation</hi> so as therein to serve God; he so <hi type="italic">served</hi> and <hi type="italic">pleased men (as whatever the king did pleased the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.36">2 Sam. iii. 36</reference>), as still to keep himself the faithful servant of God. See <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Gal. i. 10</reference>. He served the good of men, but did not serve the will of men.
