Or, by the will of God's providence so ordering it, qualifying him for, and calling him to, a public station, he <hi type="italic">served his own generation;</hi> for every creature is that to us which God makes it to be. David was a great blessing to the age wherein he lived; he was the <hi type="italic">servant</hi> of his generation: many are the curse, and plague, and burden of their generation. Even those that are in a lower and narrower sphere must look upon it that they live to <hi type="italic">serve their generation;</hi> and those that will do good in the world must make themselves <hi type="italic">servants of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19">1 Cor. ix. 19</reference>. We were not born for ourselves, but are members of communities, to which we must study to be serviceable. Yet here is the difference between David and Christ, that David was to serve only his own generation, that generation in which he lived, and therefore when he had done what he had to do, and written what he had to write, he died, and continued in the grave; but Christ (not by his writings or words upon record only as David, but by his personal agency) was to serve <hi type="italic">all</hi> generations, must ever live to reign over the house of Jacob, not as David, for forty years, but for all ages, as long as the sun and moon endure, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">Ps. lxxxix. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.36">36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.37">37</reference>. His throne must be as the days of heaven, and all generations must be blessed in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Ps. lxxii. 17</reference>. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] His death: <hi type="italic">He fell asleep.</hi> Death is a sleep, a quiet rest, to those who, while they lived, laboured in the service of God and their generation. Observe, He did not fall asleep till he had served his generation, till he had done the work for which God raised him up. God's servants have their work assigned them; and, when they have <hi type="italic">accomplished as a hireling their day,</hi> then, and not till then, they are called to rest. God's witnesses never die till they have finished their testimony; and then <hi type="italic">the sleep,</hi> the death, <hi type="italic">of the labouring man will be sweet.</hi> David was not permitted to build the temple, and therefore when he had made preparation for it, which was the service he was designed to, he fell asleep, and left the work to Solomon. [<hi type="italic">c.</hi>] His burial: <hi type="italic">He was laid to his fathers.</hi> Though he was buried in <hi type="italic">the city of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.10">1 Kings ii. 10</reference>), and not in the sepulchre of Jesse his father in Bethlehem, yet he might be said to be <hi type="italic">laid to his fathers;</hi> for the grave, in general, is the habitation of our fathers, of those that are gone before us, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.19">Ps. xlix. 19</reference>. [<hi type="italic">d.</hi>] His continuance in the grave: <hi type="italic">He saw corruption.</hi> We are sure he did not rise again; this Peter insists upon when he freely speaks of the patriarch David (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.29">ch. ii. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">He is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day.</hi> He saw corruption, and therefore that promise could not have its accomplishment in him. But, <div eID="gen29573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29574" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It was accomplished in the Lord Jesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">He whom God raised again saw no corruption;</hi> for it was in him that the sure mercies were to be reserved for us. He rose the third day, and therefore did not see corruption then; and he rose to die no more, and therefore never did. Of him therefore the promise must be understood, and no other. <div eID="gen29574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29575" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> Having given them this account of the Lord Jesus, he comes to make application of it. <div eID="gen29575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29576" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) In the midst of his discourse, to engage their attention, he had told his hearers that they were concerned in all this (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.26">v. 26</reference>): "<hi type="italic">To you is the word of this salvation sent,</hi> to you first. If you by your unbelief make it a word of rejection to you, you may thank yourselves; but it is sent to you for a word of salvation; if it be not so, it is your own fault." Let them not peevishly argue that because it was sent to the Gentiles, who had no communion with them, therefore it was not sent to them; for to them it was sent in the first place. "<hi type="italic">To you men</hi> this is sent, and not to the angels that sinned. To you living men, and not to the congregation of the dead and damned, whose day of grace is over." He therefore speaks to them with tenderness and respect: You are <hi type="italic">men and brethren;</hi> and so we are to look upon all those that stand fair with us for the great salvation as having the word of salvation sent to them. Those to whom he does by warrant from heaven here bring the <hi type="italic">word of salvation</hi> are, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] The native Jews, Hebrews of the Hebrews, as Paul himself was: "<hi type="italic">Children of the stock of Abraham,</hi> though a degenerate race, yet to you is this word of salvation sent; nay, it is therefore sent to you, to save you from your sins." It is an advantage to be of a good stock; for, though salvation does not always follow the children of godly parents, yet the word of salvation does: <hi type="italic">Abraham will command his children and his house-hold after him.</hi> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The proselytes, the Gentiles by birth, that were in some degree brought over to the Jews' religion: "<hi type="italic">Whosoever among you that feareth God.</hi> You that have a sense of natural religion, and have subjected yourselves to the laws of that, and taken hold of the comforts of that, <hi type="italic">to you is the word of this salvation sent;</hi> you need the further discoveries and directions of revealed religion, are prepared for them, and will bid them welcome, and therefore shall certainly be welcome to take the benefit of them." <div eID="gen29576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29577" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) In the close of his discourse he applies what he had said concerning Christ to his hearers. He had told them a long story concerning <hi type="italic">this Jesus;</hi> now they would be ready to ask, What is all this to us? And he tells them plainly what it is to them. <div eID="gen29577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29578" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] It will be their unspeakable advantage if they embrace Jesus Christ, and believe this word of salvation. It will relieve them where their greatest danger lies; and that is from the guilt of their sins: "<hi type="italic">Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren</hi>—we are warranted to proclaim it to you, and you are called to take notice of it." He did not stand up to preach before them, but to preach to them, and not without hopes of prevailing with them; for they are men, reasonable creatures, and capable of being argued with; they are <hi type="italic">brethren,</hi> spoken to, and dealt with, by men like themselves; not only of the same nature, but of the same nation. It is proper for the preachers of the gospel to call their hearers brethren, as speaking familiarly to them, and with an affectionate concern for their welfare, and as being equally interested with them in the gospel they preach. Let all that hear the gospel of Christ know these two things—<hi type="italic">1st,</hi> That it is an act of indemnity granted by the King of kings to the children of men, who stand attainted at his bar of treason against his crown and dignity; and it is for and in consideration of the mediation of Christ between God and man that this act of grace is passed and proclaimed (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">"Through this man,</hi> who died and rose again, <hi type="italic">is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins.</hi> We have to tell you, in God's name, that your sins, though many and great, may be forgiven, and how it is come about that they may be so, without any injury to God's honour, and how you may obtain the forgiveness of your sins. We are to preach repentance for the remission of sins, and divine grace giving both <hi type="italic">repentance and remission of sins.</hi> The remission of sins is <hi type="italic">through this man.</hi> By his merit it was purchased, in his name it is offered, and by his authority it is bestowed; and therefore you are concerned to be acquainted with him, and interested in him. We preach to you <hi type="italic">the forgiveness of sins.</hi> That is the salvation we bring you, the word of God; and therefore you ought to bid us welcome and look upon us as your friends, and messengers of good tidings." <hi type="italic">2ndly,</hi> That it does that for us which the law of Moses could not do. The Jews were jealous for the law, and because it prescribed expiatory and pacificatory sacrifices, and a great variety of purifications, fancied they might be justified by it before God. "No," saith Paul, "be it known to you that it is by Christ only that <hi type="italic">those who believe in him,</hi> and none else, are <hi type="italic">justified from all things,</hi> from all the guilt and stain of sin, <hi type="italic">from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.39">v. 39</reference>); therefore they ought to entertain and embrace the gospel, and not to adhere to the law in opposition to it, because the gospel is perfective, not destructive, of the law. Note, 1. The great concern of sinners it to be justified, to be acquitted from guilt and accepted as righteous in God's sight. 2. Those who are truly justified are acquitted from all their guilt; for if any be left charged upon the sinner he is undone. 3. It was impossible for a sinner to be justified by the law of Moses. Not by his moral law, for we have all broken it, and are transgressing it daily, so that instead of justifying us it condemns us. Not by his remedial law, for it was not possible that the <hi type="italic">blood of bulls and goats should take away sin,</hi> should satisfy God's offended justice, or pacify the sinner's wounded conscience. It was but a ritual and typical institution. See <reference osisRef="Heb.9.9 10.1 4">Heb. ix. 9; x. 1, 4</reference>. 4. By Jesus Christ we obtain a complete justification; for by him a complete atonement was made for sin. We are justified, not only by him as our Judge, but by him as our righteousness, <hi type="italic">the Lord our righteousness.</hi> 5. All that believe in Christ, that rely upon him and give up themselves to be ruled by him, are justified by him, and none but they. 6. What the law <hi type="italic">could not do</hi> for us, <hi type="italic">in that it was weak,</hi> that the gospel of Christ does; and therefore it was folly, out of a jealousy for the law of Moses and the honour of that institution, to conceive a jealousy of the gospel of Christ and the designs of that more perfect institution. <div eID="gen29578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29579" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] It is at their utmost peril if they reject the gospel of Christ, and turn their backs upon the offer now made them (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.40-Acts.13.41">v. 40, 41</reference>): <hi type="italic">Beware therefore;</hi> you have a fair invitation given you, look to yourselves, lest you either neglect or oppose it." Note, Those to whom the gospel is preached must see themselves upon their trial and good behaviour, and are concerned to beware lest they be found refusers of the grace offered. "Beware lest you not only come short of the blessings and benefits spoken of in the prophets as coming upon those that believe, but fall under the doom spoken of in the prophets as coming upon those that persist in unbelief: <hi type="italic">lest that come upon you which is spoken of.</hi>" Note, The threatenings are warnings ; what we are told will come upon impenitent sinners is designed to awaken us to beware lest it should come upon us. Now the prophecy referred to we have <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Hab. i. 5</reference>, where the destruction of the Jewish nation by the Chaldeans is foretold as an incredible unparalleled destruction; and this is here applied to the destruction that was coming upon that nation by the Romans, for their rejecting the gospel of Christ. The apostle follows the Septuagint translation, which reads, <hi type="italic">Behold, you despisers</hi> (for, <hi type="italic">behold, you among the heathen</hi>); because it made the text more apposite to his purpose. 1<hi type="italic">st,</hi> "Take heed lest the guilt come upon you which was spoken of in the prophets—the guilt of despising the gospel and the tenders of it, and despising the Gentiles that were advanced to partake of it. Beware lest it be said to you, <hi type="italic">Behold, you despisers.</hi>" Note, It is the ruin of many that they despise religion, they look upon it as a thing below them, and are not willing to stoop to it. 2<hi type="italic">ndly,</hi> "Take heed lest the judgment come upon you which was spoken of in the prophets: that <hi type="italic">you shall wonder and perish,</hi> that is, wonderfully perish; your perdition shall be amazing to yourselves and all about you." Those that will not wonder and be saved shall wonder and perish. Those that enjoyed the privileges of the church, and flattered themselves with a conceit that these would save them, will wonder when they find their vain presumption overruled and that their privileges do but make their condemnation the more intolerable. Let the unbelieving Jews expect that God will <hi type="italic">work a work in their days which you shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you.</hi> This may be understood as a prediction, either, 1. Of their sin, that they should be incredulous, that that great work of God, the redemption of the world by Christ, though it should be in the most solemn manner declared unto them, yet they would <hi type="italic">in no wise believe it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa. liii. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Who hath believed our report?</hi> Though it was of God's working, to whom nothing is impossible, and of his declaring, who cannot lie, yet they would not give credit to it. Those that had the honour and advantage to have this work wrought in their days had not the grace to believe it. Or, 2. Of their destruction. The dissolving of the Jewish polity, the taking of the kingdom of God from them and giving it to the Gentiles, the destruction of their holy house and city, and the dispersion of their people, was a work which one would not have believed should have ever been done, considering how much they had been the favourites of Heaven. The calamities that were brought upon them were such as were never before brought upon any people, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.21">Matt. xxiv. 21</reference>. It was said of their destruction by the Chaldeans, and it was true of their last destruction, <hi type="italic">All the inhabitants of the world would not have believed that the enemy would have entered into the gates of Jerusalem as they did,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.12">Lam. iv. 12</reference>. Thus is there a <hi type="italic">strange punishment to the workers of iniquity,</hi> especially to the despisers of Christ, <reference osisRef="Job.31.3">Job xxxi. 3</reference>.
entries.f7e34a4856159a90088a8c7ccfcc7bbceb09901e: <div eID="gen29579" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul at Antioch in Pisidia.</title> <div sID="gen29580" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">42</hi> And when the Jews were gone out of the synagogue, the Gentiles besought that these words might be preached to them the next sabbath. <hi type="super">43</hi> Now when the congregation was broken up, many of the Jews and religious proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas: who, speaking to them, persuaded them to continue in the grace of God. <hi type="super">44</hi> And the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God. <hi type="super">45</hi> But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming. <hi type="super">46</hi> Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles. <hi type="super">47</hi> For so hath the Lord commanded us, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth. <hi type="super">48</hi> And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. <hi type="super">49</hi> And the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region. <hi type="super">50</hi> But the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts. 51 But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came unto Iconium. <hi type="super">52</hi> And the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost. <div eID="gen29580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29581" type="x-p"/> The design of this story being to vindicate the apostles, especially Paul (as he doth himself at large, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1-Rom.11.36">Rom. xi.</reference>), from the reflections of the Jews upon him for preaching the gospel to the Gentiles, it is here observed that he proceeded therein with all the caution imaginable, and upon due consideration, of which we have here an instance. <div eID="gen29581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29582" type="x-p"/> I. There were some of the Jews that were so incensed against the preaching of the gospel, not to the Gentiles, but to themselves, that they would not bear to hear it, but <hi type="italic">went out of the synagogue</hi> while Paul was preaching (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.42">v. 42</reference>), in contempt of him and his doctrine, and to the disturbance of the congregation. It is probable they whispered among themselves, exciting one another to it, and did it by consent. Now this bespoke, 1. An open infidelity, as plain a profession of unbelief as coming to hear the gospel is of faith. They thus publicly avowed their contempt of Christ and of his doctrine and law, were not ashamed, neither could they blush; and they thus endeavoured to beget prejudices in the minds of others against the gospel; they went out to draw others to follow their pernicious ways. 2. An obstinate infidelity. They went out of the synagogue, not only to show that they did not believe the gospel, but because they were resolved they would not, and therefore got out of the hearing of those things that had a tendency to convince them. They stopped their ears like the deaf adder. Justly therefore was the gospel taken from them, when they first took themselves from it, and turned themselves out of the church before they were turned out of it. For it is certainly true that God never leaves any till they first leave him. <div eID="gen29582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29583" type="x-p"/> II. The Gentiles were as willing to hear the gospel as those rude and ill-conditioned Jews were to get out of the hearing of it: <hi type="italic">They besought that these words,</hi> or words to this effect, <hi type="italic">might be preached to them the next sabbath;</hi> in <hi type="italic">the week between,</hi> so some take it; on the second and fifth days of the week, which in some synagogues were their lecture days. But it appears (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.44">v. 44</reference>) that it was the next sabbath day that they came together. They begged, 1. That the same offer might be made to them that was made to the Jews. Paul in this sermon had brought the word of salvation to the Jews and proselytes, but had taken no notice of the Gentiles; and therefore they begged that forgiveness of sins through Christ might be preached to them, as it was to the Jews. The Jews' leavings, nay, loathings, were their longings. This justifies Paul in his preaching to them, that he was invited to it, as Peter was sent for to Cornelius. Who could refuse to break the bread of life to those who begged so hard for it, and to give that to the poor at the door which the children at the table threw under their feet? 2. That the same instructions might be given to them. They had heard the doctrine of Christ, but did not understand it at the first hearing, nor could they remember all that they had heard, and therefore they begged it might be preached to them again. Note, It is good to have the word of Christ repeated to us. What we have heard we should desire to hear again, that it may take deep root in us, and the nail that is driven may be clenched and be <hi type="italic">as a nail in a sure place.</hi> To hear <hi type="italic">the same things</hi> should not be grievous, because it is safe, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>. It aggravates the bad disposition of the Jews that the Gentiles desired to hear that often which they were not willing to hear once; and commends the good disposition of the Gentiles that they did not follow the bad example which the Jews set them. <div eID="gen29583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29584" type="x-p"/> III. There were some, nay, there were many, both of Jews and proselytes, that were wrought upon by the preaching of the gospel. Those who aggravated the matter of the Jews' rejection by the preaching of the gospel, cried out, as is usual in such cases, "They have cast away, and cast off, all the people of God." "Nay," says Paul, "it is not so; for abundance of the Jews have embraced Christ, and are taken in;" himself for one, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">5</reference>. So it was here: <hi type="italic">Many of the Jews and religious proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas,</hi> and received further instructions and encouragement from them. 1. They submitted to the grace of God, and were admitted to the benefit and comfort of it, which is implied in their being exhorted to continue in it. They <hi type="italic">followed Paul and Barnabas;</hi> they became their disciples, or rather the disciples of Christ, whose agents they were. Those that join themselves to Christ will join themselves to his ministers, and follow them. And Paul and Barnabas, though they were sent to the Gentiles, yet bade those of the Jews welcome that were willing to come under their instructions, such hearty well-wishers were they to all the Jews and their friends, if they pleased. 2. They were exhorted and encouraged to persevere herein: <hi type="italic">Paul and Barnabas, speaking to them</hi> with all the freedom and friendship imaginable, <hi type="italic">persuaded them to continue in the grace of God,</hi> to hold fast that which they had received, to continue in their belief of the gospel of grace, their dependence upon the Spirit of grace, and their attendance upon the means of grace. And the grace of God shall not be wanting to those who thus continue in it. <div eID="gen29584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29585" type="x-p"/> IV. There was a cheerful attendance upon the preaching of the gospel the <hi type="italic">next sabbath day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.44">v. 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">Almost the whole city</hi> (the generality of whom were Gentiles) <hi type="italic">came together to hear the word of God.</hi> 1. It is probable that Paul and Barnabas were not idle in the week-days, but took all opportunities in the week between (as some think the Gentiles desired) to bring them acquainted with Christ, and to raise their expectations from him. They did a great deal of service to the gospel in private discourse and conversation, as well as in their public sermons. Wisdom cried in the chief places of concourse, and the opening of the gates, as well as in the synagogues, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 20, 21</reference>. 2. This brought a vast concourse of people to the synagogue on the sabbath day. Some came out of curiosity, the thing being new; others longing to see what the Jews would do upon the second tender of the gospel to them; and many who had heard something of the word of God came to hear more, and to hear it, <hi type="italic">not as the word of men but as the word of God,</hi> by which we must be ruled and judged. Now this justified Paul in preaching to the Gentiles, that he met with the most encouraging auditors among them. There <hi type="italic">the fields were white to the harvest,</hi> and therefore why should he not there put in his sickle? <div eID="gen29585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29586" type="x-p"/> V. The Jews were enraged at this; and not only would not receive the gospel themselves, but were filled with indignation at those that crowded after it (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.45">v. 45</reference>): <hi type="italic">When the Jews saw the multitudes,</hi> and considered what an encouragement it was to Paul to go on in his work when he saw the people thus flying like doves to their windows, and what probability there was that among these multitudes some would be, without doubt, wrought upon, and probably the greater part, to embrace Christ—this <hi type="italic">filled them with envy.</hi> 1. They grudged the interest the apostles had in the people, were vexed to see the synagogue so full when they were going to preach. This was the same spirit that worked in the Pharisees towards Christ; they were cut to the heart when they saw <hi type="italic">the whole world go after him.</hi> When the kingdom of heaven was opened they not only would not go in themselves, but were angry with those that did. 2. They opposed the doctrine the apostles preached: <hi type="italic">They spoke against those things that were spoken by Paul,</hi> cavilled at them, started objections against them, finding some fault or other with every thing he said, <hi type="italic">contradicting and blaspheming;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">antelegon antilegontes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">contradicting, they contradicted.</hi> They did it with the utmost spite and rage imaginable: they persisted in their contradiction, and nothing would silence them, they contradicted for contradiction-sake, and denied that which was most evident; and, when they could find no colour of objection, they broke out into ill language against Christ and his gospel, blaspheming him and it. From the language of the carnal man that receives not the things of the Spirit of God, and therefore contradicts them, they proceed to the language of incarnate devils, and blaspheme them. Commonly those who begin with contradicting end with blaspheming. <div eID="gen29586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29587" type="x-p"/> VI. The apostles hereupon solemnly and openly declare themselves discharged from their obligations to the Jews, and at liberty to bring the word of salvation to the Gentiles, even by the tacit consent of the Jews themselves. Never let the Jew lay the fault of the carrying of the kingdom of God to the Gentiles upon the apostles, for that complaint of theirs is for ever silenced by their own act and deed, for what they did here is for ever a bar to it. "Tender and refusal (we say) are good payment in law." The Jews had the tender of the gospel, and did refuse it, and therefore ought not to say any thing against the Gentiles having it. In declaring this, it is said (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.46">v. 46</reference>), <hi type="italic">Paul and Barnabas waxed bold,</hi> more bold than they had been while they were shy of looking favourably upon the Gentiles, for fear of giving offence to the Jews, and laying a stumbling-block in their way. Note, There is a time for the preachers of the gospel to show as much of the boldness of the lion as of the wisdom of the serpent and the harmlessness of the dove. When the adversaries of Christ's cause begin to be daring, it is not for its advocates to be timid. While there is any hope of working upon those that oppose themselves they must be <hi type="italic">instructed with meekness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2 Tim. ii. 25</reference>); but, when that method has long been tried in vain, we must wax bold, and tell them what will be the issue of their opposition. The impudence of the enemies of the gospel, instead of frightening, should rather embolden its friends; for they are sure that they have a good cause, and they know in whom they have trusted to bear them out. Now Paul and Barnabas, having made the Jews a fair offer of gospel grace, here give them fair notice of their bringing it to the Gentiles, <hi type="italic">if by any means</hi> (as Paul says <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Rom. xi. 14</reference>) <hi type="italic">they might provoke them to emulation.</hi> 1. They own that the Jews were entitled to the first offer: "<hi type="italic">It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you,</hi> to whom the promise was made, to you <hi type="italic">of the lost sheep of the house of Israel,</hi> to whom Christ reckoned himself first sent." And his charge to the preachers of his gospel to <hi type="italic">begin at Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>) was a tacit direction to all that went into other countries to begin with the Jews, <hi type="italic">to whom pertained the giving of the law,</hi> and therefore the preaching of the gospel. <hi type="italic">Let the children first be served,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.27">Mark vii. 27</reference>. 2. They charge them with the refusal of it: "<hi type="italic">You put it from you;</hi> you will not accept of it; nay, you will not so much as bear the offer of it, but take it as an affront to you." If men put the gospel from them, God justly takes it from them; why should manna be given to those that loathe it and call it <hi type="italic">light bread,</hi> or the privileges of the gospel forced on those that put them away, and say, <hi type="italic">We have no part in David?</hi> Herein they <hi type="italic">judge themselves unworthy of everlasting life.</hi> In one sense we must all judge ourselves unworthy of everlasting life, for there is nothing in us, nor done by us, by which we can pretend to merit it, and we must be made sensible of this; but here the meaning is, "You discover, or make it to appear, that you are not meet for eternal life; you throw away all your claims and give up your pretensions to it; since you will not take it from his hands, into whose hand the Father has given it, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">krinete,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">you do,</hi> in effect, <hi type="italic">pass this judgment</hi> upon yourselves, and <hi type="italic">out of your own mouth you shall be judged;</hi> you will not have it by Christ, by whom alone it is to be had, and so shall your doom be, you shall not have it at all." 3. Upon this they ground their preaching the gospel to the uncircumcised: "Since you will not accept eternal life as it is offered, our way is plain, <hi type="italic">Lo, we turn to the Gentiles.</hi> If one will not, another will. If those that were first invited to the wedding-feast will not come, we must invite out of the highways and hedges those that will, for <hi type="italic">the wedding must be furnished with guests.</hi> If he that is next of kin will not do the kinsman's part, he must not complain that another will," <reference osisRef="Ruth.4.4">Ruth iv. 4</reference>. 4. They justify themselves in this by a divine warrant (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.47">v. 47</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For so hath the Lord commanded us;</hi> the Lord Jesus gave us directions to witness to him in Jerusalem and Judea first, and after that <hi type="italic">to the utmost part of the earth,</hi> to preach the gospel to <hi type="italic">every creature,</hi> to <hi type="italic">disciple all nations.</hi>" This is according to what was foretold in the Old-Testament. When the Messiah, in the prospect of the Jews' infidelity, was ready to say, <hi type="italic">I have laboured in vain,</hi> he was told, to his satisfaction, that though <hi type="italic">Israel were not gathered,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">he should be glorious,</hi> that his blood should not be shed in vain, nor his purchase made in vain, nor his doctrine preached in vain, nor his Spirit sent in vain—"For <hi type="italic">I have set thee,</hi> not only raised thee up, but established thee, to be <hi type="italic">a light of the Gentiles,</hi> not only a shining light for a time, but a standing light, set thee for a light, <hi type="italic">that thou shouldst be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.</hi>" Note, (1.) Christ is not only the Saviour, but the salvation, is himself our righteousness, and life, and strength. (2.) Wherever Christ is designed to be salvation, he is set up to be a light; he enlightens the understanding, and so saves the soul. (3.) He is, and is to be, light and salvation to the Gentiles, to the ends of the earth. Those of every nation shall be welcome to him, some of every nation have heard of him (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.18">Rom. x. 18</reference>), and all nations shall at length become his kingdom. This prophecy has had its accomplishment in part in the setting up of the kingdom of Christ in this island of ours, which lies, as it were, in the <hi type="italic">ends of the earth,</hi> a corner of the world, and shall be accomplished more and more when the time comes for the <hi type="italic">bringing in of the fulness of the Gentiles.</hi> <div eID="gen29587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29588" type="x-p"/> VII. The Gentiles cheerfully embraced that which the Jews scornfully rejected, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.48-Acts.13.49">v. 48, 49</reference>. Never was land lost for want of heirs; <hi type="italic">through the fall of the Jews, salvation is come to the Gentiles:</hi> the <hi type="italic">casting off of them was the reconciling of the world, and the diminishing of them the riches of the Gentiles;</hi> so the apostle shows at large, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.11-Rom.11.12">Rom. xi. 11, 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">15</reference>. The Jews, the natural branches, were broken off, and the Gentiles, that were branches of the wild olive, were thereupon grafted in, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">v. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.19">19</reference>. Now here we are told how the Gentiles welcomed this happy turn in their favour. <div eID="gen29588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29589" type="x-p"/> 1. They took the comfort of it: <hi type="italic">When they heard this they were glad.</hi> It was good news to them that they might have admission into covenant and communion with God by a clearer, nearer, and better way than submitting to the ceremonial law, and being proselyted to the Jewish religion—that the partition-wall was taken down and they were as welcome to the benefits of the Messiah's kingdom as the Jews themselves, and might share in their promise, without coming under their yoke. This was indeed <hi type="italic">glad tidings of great joy to all people.</hi> Note, Our being put into a possibility of salvation, and a capacity for it, ought to be the matter of our rejoicing; when the Gentiles did but hear that the offers of grace should be made them, the word of grace preached to them, and the means of grace afforded them, <hi type="italic">they were glad.</hi> "Now there is some hope for us." Many grieve under doubts whether they have an interest in Christ or no, when they should be rejoicing that they have an interest in him; the golden sceptre is held out to them, and they are invited to come and touch the top of it. <div eID="gen29589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29590" type="x-p"/> 2. They gave God the praise of it: <hi type="italic">They glorified the word of the Lord;</hi> that is, Christ (so some), the essential Word; they entertained a profound veneration for him, and expressed the high thoughts they had of him. Or, rather, <hi type="italic">the gospel;</hi> the more they knew of it, the more they admired it. Oh! what a light, what a power, what a treasure, does this gospel bring along with it! How excellent are its truths, its precepts, its promises! How far transcending all other institutions! How plainly divine and heavenly is its origin! Thus they <hi type="italic">glorified the word of the Lord,</hi> and it is this which he has himself <hi type="italic">magnified above all his name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.2">Ps. cxxxviii. 2</reference>), and will <hi type="italic">magnify</hi> and <hi type="italic">make honourable,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">Isa. xlii. 21</reference>. They glorified the word of the Lord, (1.) Because now the knowledge of it was diffused and not confined to the Jews only. Note, It is the glory of the word of the Lord that the further it spreads the brighter it shines, which shows it to be not like the light of the candle, but like that of the sun when he goes forth in his strength. (2.) Because now the knowledge of it was brought to them. Note, Those speak best of the honour of the word of the Lord that speak experimentally, that have themselves been subdued by its power, and comforted by its sweetness. <div eID="gen29590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29591" type="x-p"/> 3. Many of them became, not only professors of the Christian faith, but sincerely obedient to the faith: <hi type="italic">As many as were ordained to eternal life believed.</hi> God by his Spirit wrought true faith in those for whom he had in his councils from everlasting designed a happiness to everlasting. (1.) Those believed to whom God gave grace to believe, whom by a secret and mighty operation he brought into subjection to the gospel of Christ, and made willing in the day of his power. Those came to Christ whom the Father drew, and to whom the Spirit made the gospel call effectual. It is called <hi type="italic">the faith of the operation of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col. ii. 12</reference>), and is said to be <hi type="italic">wrought by the same power that raised up Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19-Eph.1.20">Eph. i. 19, 20</reference>. (2.) God gave this grace to believe to all those among them who were ordained to eternal life (for <hi type="italic">whom he had predestinated, them he also called,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.30">Rom. viii. 30</reference>); or, <hi type="italic">as many as were disposed to eternal life,</hi> as many as had a concern about their eternal state, and aimed to make sure of eternal life, believed in Christ, in whom God hath treasured up that life (<reference osisRef="1John.5.11">1 John v. 11</reference>), and who is the only way to it; and it was the grace of God that wrought it in them. Thus all those captives, and those only, took the benefit of Cyrus's proclamation, <hi type="italic">whose spirit God had raised up to build the house of the Lord which is in Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5">Ezra i. 5</reference>. Those will be brought to believe in Christ that by his grace are well disposed to eternal life, and make this their aim. <div eID="gen29591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29592" type="x-p"/> 4. When they believed they did what they could to spread the knowledge of Christ and his gospel among their neighbours (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">And the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region.</hi> When it was received with so much satisfaction in the chief city, it soon spread into all parts of the country. Those new converts were themselves ready to communicate to others that which they were so full of themselves. <hi type="italic">The Lord gave the word, and then great was the company of those that published it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.11">Ps. lxviii. 11</reference>. Those that have become acquainted with Christ themselves will do what they can to bring others acquainted with him. Those in great and rich cities that have received the gospel should not think to engross it, as if, like learning and philosophy, it were only to be the entertainment of the more polite and elevated part of mankind, but should do what they can to get it published in the country among the ordinary sort of people, the poor and unlearned, who have souls to be saved as well as they. <div eID="gen29592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29593" type="x-p"/> VIII. Paul and Barnabas, having sown the seeds of a Christian church there, quitted the place, and went to do the like else-where. We read not any thing of their working miracles here, to confirm their doctrine, and to convince people of the truth of it; for, though God then did ordinarily make use of that method of conviction, yet he could, when he pleased, do his work without it; and begetting faith by the immediate influence of his Spirit was itself the greatest miracle to those in whom it was wrought. Yet, it is probable that they did work miracles, for we find they did in the next place they came to, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.3">ch. xiv. 3</reference>. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen29593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29594" type="x-p"/> 1. How <hi type="italic">the unbelieving Jews</hi> expelled the apostles out of that country. They first turned their back upon them, and then <hi type="italic">lifted up the heel against them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.50">v. 50</reference>): <hi type="italic">They raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas,</hi> excited the mob to persecute them in <hi type="italic">their</hi> way by insulting their persons as they went along the streets; excited the magistrates to persecute them in <hi type="italic">their</hi> way, by imprisoning and punishing them. When <hi type="italic">they could not resist the wisdom and spirit wherewith they spoke,</hi> they had recourse to these brutish methods, the last refuge of an obstinate infidelity. Satan and his agents are most exasperated against the preachers of the gospel when they see them go on successfully, and therefore then will be sure to raise persecution against them. Thus it has been the common lot of the best men in the world to suffer ill for doing well, to be persecuted instead of being preferred for the good services they have done to mankind. Observe, (1.) What method the Jews took to give them trouble: <hi type="italic">They stirred up the devout and honourable women</hi> against them. They could not make any considerable interest themselves, but they applied to some ladies of quality in the city, that were well affected to the Jewish religion, and were proselytes of the gate, therefore called <hi type="italic">devout women.</hi> These, according to the genius of their sex, were zealous in their way, and bigoted; and it was easy, by false stories and misrepresentations, to incense them against the gospel of Christ, as if it had been destructive of all religion, of which really it is perfective. It is good to see honourable women devout, and well affected to religious worship: The less they have to do in the world, the more they should do for their souls, and the more time they should spend in communion with God; but it is sad when, under colour of devotion to God, they conceive an enmity to Christ, as those here mentioned. What! women persecutors! Can they forget the tenderness and compassion of their sex? What! honourable women! Can they thus stain their honour, and disgrace themselves, and do so mean a thing? But, which is strangest of all, devout women! Will they kill Christ's servants, and think therein they do God service? Let those therefore that have zeal see that it be according to knowledge. By these devout and honourable women they stirred up likewise <hi type="italic">the chief men of the city,</hi> the magistrates and the rulers, who had power in their hands and set them against the apostles, and they had so little consideration as to suffer themselves to be made the tools of this ill-natured party, who <hi type="italic">would neither go into the kingdom of heaven themselves nor suffer those who were entering to go in.</hi> (2.) How far they carried it, so far that <hi type="italic">they expelled them out of their coasts;</hi> they banished them, ordered them to be carried, as we say, from constable to constable, till they were forced out of their jurisdiction; so that it was not by fear, but downright violence, that they were driven out. This was one method which the overruling providence of God took to keep the first planters of the church from staying too long at a place; as <reference osisRef="Matt.10.23">Matt. x. 23</reference>, <hi type="italic">When they persecute you in one city flee to another,</hi> that thus you may the sooner <hi type="italic">go over the cities of Israel.</hi> This was likewise a method God took to make those that were well disposed the more warmly affected towards the apostles; for it is natural to us to pity those that are persecuted, to think the better of those that suffer when we know they suffer unjustly, and to be the more ready to help them. The expelling of the apostles out of their coasts made people inquisitive what evil they had done, and perhaps raised them more friends than conniving at them in their coasts would have done. <div eID="gen29594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29595" type="x-p"/> 2. How the apostles abandoned and rejected the unbelieving Jews (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.51">v. 51</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shook off the dust of their feet against them.</hi> When they went out of the city they used this ceremony in the sight of those that sat in the gate; or, when they went out of the borders of their country, in the sight of those that were sent to see the country rid of them. Hereby, (1.) They declared that they would have no more to do with them, would take nothing that was theirs; for <hi type="italic">they sought not theirs, but them.</hi> Dust they are, and let them keep their dust to themselves, it shall not cleave to them. (2.) They expressed their detestation of their infidelity, and that, though they were Jews by birth, yet, having rejected the gospel of Christ, they were in their eyes no better than heathen and profane. As Jews and Gentiles, if they believe, are equally acceptable to God and good men; so, if they do not, they are equally abominable. (3.) Thus they set them at defiance, and expressed their contempt of them and their malice, which they looked upon as impotent. It was as much as to say, "Do your worst, we do not fear you; we know whom we serve and whom we have trusted." (4.) Thus they left a testimony behind them that they had had a fair offer made them of the grace of the gospel, which shall be proved against them in the day of judgment. This dust will prove that the preachers of the gospel had been among them, but were expelled by them. Thus Christ had ordered them to do, and for this reason, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.14">Matt. x. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.5">Luke ix. 5</reference>. When <hi type="italic">they left them, they came to Iconium,</hi> not so much for safety, as for work. <div eID="gen29595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29596" type="x-p"/> 3. What frame they left the new converts in <hi type="italic">at Antioch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.52">v. 52</reference>): <hi type="italic">The disciples,</hi> when they saw with what courage and cheerfulness Paul and Barnabas not only bore the indignities that were done them, but went on with their work notwithstanding, they were in like manner inspirited. (1.) They were very cheerful. One would have expected that when Paul and Barnabas were expelled out of their coasts, and perhaps forbidden to return upon pain of death, the disciples would have been full of grief and full of fear, looking for no other than that, if the planters of Christianity go, the plantation would soon come to nothing; or that it would be their turn next to be banished the country, and to them it would be more grievous, for it was their own. But no; <hi type="italic">they were filled with joy</hi> in Christ, had such a satisfactory assurance of Christ's carrying on and perfecting his own work in them and among them, and that either he would screen them from trouble or bear them up under it, that all their fears were swallowed up in their believing joys. (2.) They were courageous, wonderfully animated with a holy resolution to cleave to Christ, whatever difficulties they met with. This seems especially to be meant by <hi type="italic">their being filled with the Holy Ghost,</hi> for the same expression is used of Peter's boldness (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.8">ch. iv. 8</reference>), and Stephen's (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.55">ch. vii. 55</reference>), and Paul's, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.9">ch. xiii. 9</reference>. The more we relish the comforts and encouragements we meet with in the power of godliness, and the fuller our hearts are of them, the better prepared we are to face the difficulties we meet with in the profession of godliness.  <chapter eID="Acts.13"/> <div eID="gen29596" type="x-p"/>

entries.3580974a5fd87d57ab87665ca616ba88acd1a36e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15857"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <div sID="gen30539" type="x-p"/> PAUL'S FIRST MISSIONARY JOURNEY: In Company with Barnabas. <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1-Acts.14.28">Ac 13:1-14:28</reference>.<div eID="gen30539" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.13.1-Acts.13.3">Ac 13:1-3</reference>. Barnabas and Saul, Divinely Called to Labor among the Gentiles, Are Set Apart and Sent Forth by the Church at Antioch.</title> <div sID="gen30540" type="x-p"/> The first seven chapters of this book might be entitled, The Church among the Jews; the next five (chapters eight through twelve), The Church in Transition from Jews to Gentiles; and the last sixteen (chapters thirteen through twenty-eight), The Church among the Gentiles [Baumgarten]. "Though Christianity had already spread beyond the limits of Palestine, still the Church continued a stranger to formal missionary effort. Casual occurrences, particularly the persecution at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.2">Ac 8:2</reference>), had hitherto brought about the diffusion of the Gospel. It was from Antioch that teachers were first sent forth with the definite purpose of spreading Christianity, and organizing churches, with regular institutions (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">Ac 14:23</reference>)" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen30540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15857"/><hi type="bold">1. there were ... certain prophets--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Acts.11.27">Ac 11:27</reference>).<div eID="gen30541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and teachers; as Barnabas, &c.--</hi>implying that there were others there, besides; but, according to what appears the true reading, the meaning is simply that those here mentioned were in the Church at Antioch as prophets and teachers.<div eID="gen30542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Simeon ... Niger--</hi>of whom nothing is known.<div eID="gen30543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lucius of Cyrene--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.2.20">Ac 2:20</reference>). He is mentioned, in <reference osisRef="Rom.16.21">Ro 16:21</reference>, as one of Paul's kinsmen.<div eID="gen30544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Manaen--</hi>or Menahem, the name of one of the kings of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.14">2Ki 15:14</reference>).<div eID="gen30545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which had been brought up with--</hi>or, the foster brother of.<div eID="gen30546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Herod the tetrarch--</hi>that is, Antipas, who was himself "brought up with a certain private person at Rome" [Josephus, Antiquities, 17.1,3]. How differently did these two foster brothers turn out--the one, abandoned to a licentious life and stained with the blood of the most distinguished of God's prophets, though not without his fits of reformation and seasons of remorse; the other, a devoted disciple of the Lord Jesus and prophet of the Church at Antioch! But this is only what may be seen in every age: "Even so, Father, for so it seemeth good in Thy sight.' If the courtier, whose son, at the point of death, was healed by our Lord (<reference osisRef="John.4.46">Joh 4:46</reference>) was of Herod's establishment, while Susanna's husband was his steward (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.3">Lu 8:3</reference>), his foster brother's becoming a Christian and a prophet is something remarkable.<div eID="gen30547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Saul--</hi>last of all, but soon to become first. Henceforward this book is almost exclusively occupied with him; and his impress on the New Testament, on Christendom, and on the world is paramount. <div eID="gen30548" type="x-p"/>
entries.df656fcfe34a419c006396c80c30ae75f288edde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15858"/><div sID="gen30549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15858"/><hi type="bold">2. As they ministered to the Lord--</hi>The word denotes the performance of official duties of any kind, and was used to express the priestly functions under the Old Testament. Here it signifies the corresponding ministrations of the Christian Church.<div eID="gen30549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and fasted--</hi>As this was done in other cases on special occasions (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">Ac 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">14, 23</reference>), it is not improbable that they had been led to expect some such prophetic announcement at this time.<div eID="gen30550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Holy Ghost said--</hi>through some of the prophets mentioned in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1">Ac 13:1</reference>.<div eID="gen30551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Separate me--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Rom.1.1">Ro 1:1</reference>.<div eID="gen30552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the work whereunto I have called them--</hi>by some communication, perhaps, to themselves: in the case of Saul at least, such a designation was indicated from the first (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.21">Ac 22:21</reference>). Note.--While the personality of the Holy Ghost is manifest from this language, His supreme divinity will appear equally so by comparing it with <reference osisRef="Heb.5.4">He 5:4</reference>. <div eID="gen30553" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1547d6908b06b02db5f05fb9758b59372f6e235: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15859"/><div sID="gen30554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15859"/><hi type="bold">3. laid their hands on them--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Acts.6.6">Ac 6:6</reference>)--"recommending them to the grace of God for the work which they had to fulfil" (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.26">Ac 14:26</reference>).<div eID="gen30554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30555" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent them away--</hi>with the double call--of the Spirit first, and next of the Church. So clothed, their mission is thus described: "They being sent forth by the Holy Ghost." Have we not here for all time the true principle of appointment to sacred offices? <div eID="gen30555" type="x-p"/>
entries.3af2bb2abd5b6a820e2e980cda942c9a5c3476b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15860"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.13.4-Acts.13.12">Ac 13:4-12</reference>. Arriving in Cyprus They Preach in the Synagogues of Salamis--At Paphos, Elymas Is Struck Blind, and the Governor of the Island Is Converted.</title> <div sID="gen30556" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15860"/><hi type="bold">4-5. departed unto Seleucia--</hi>the seaport of Antioch, from which it lay nearly due west fifteen miles, and five from the Mediterranean shore, on the river Orontes.<div eID="gen30556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thence sailed to Cyprus--</hi>whose high mountain summits are easily seen in clear weather from the coast [Colonel Chesney in Howson]. "Four reasons may have induced them to turn in first to this island: (1) Its nearness to the mainland; (2) It was the native place of Barnabas, and since the time when Andrew found his brother Simon, and brought him to Jesus, and "Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus," family ties had not been without effect on the progress of the Gospel. (3) It could not be unnatural to suppose that the truth would be welcomed in Cyprus when brought by Barnabas and his kinsman Mark, to their own connections or friends. The Jews were numerous in Salamis. By sailing to that city, they were following the track of the synagogues; and though their mission was chiefly to the Gentiles, their surest course for reaching them was through the proselytes and Hellenizing Jews. (4) Some of the Cypriotes were already Christians. Indeed, no one place out of Palestine, except Antioch, had been so honorably associated with the work of successful evangelization" [Howson]. <div eID="gen30557" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8a81c9059b09ed4d320fb898b970a5a8ec44b46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15862"/><div sID="gen30561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15862"/><hi type="bold">6. when they had gone through the isle unto Paphos--</hi>on the opposite or west side of the island, about one hundred miles by land, along the south coast; the Roman capital, where the governor resided.<div eID="gen30561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they found a ... sorcerer--</hi>one of a numerous class of impostors who, at this time of general unbelief, were encouraged even by cultivated Romans. <div eID="gen30562" type="x-p"/>
entries.80b371754a72980dbee222b0ea014f64927d9731: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15863"/><div sID="gen30563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15863"/><hi type="bold">7. Which was with the deputy--</hi>properly, "the proconsul." This name was reserved for the governors of settled provinces, which were placed under the Roman Senate, and is never given in the New Testament to Pilate, Felix, or Festus, who were but procurators, or subordinate administrators of unsettled, imperial, military provinces. Now as Augustus reserved Cyprus for himself, its governor would in that case have been not a proconsul, but simply a procurator, had not the emperor afterwards restored it to the Senate, as a Roman historian [Dio Cassius] expressly states. In most striking confirmation of this minute accuracy of the sacred historian, coins have actually been found in the island, stamped with the names of proconsuls, both in Greek and Latin [Akerman, Numismatic Illustrations of the New Testament]. (Grotius and Bengel, not aware of this, have missed the mark here).<div eID="gen30563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sergius Paulus, a prudent man--</hi>an intelligent man, who thirsting for truth, sent for Barnabas and Saul, desiring ("earnestly desiring") to hear the Word of God. <div eID="gen30564" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d1dd47856bcd7a0b06b88ef1be91b0da5bba779: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15864"/><div sID="gen30565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15864"/><hi type="bold">8-12. But Elymas--</hi>or "the wise."<div eID="gen30565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for so is his name by interpretation--</hi>the word is from the Arabic.<div eID="gen30566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">withstood them--</hi>perceiving, probably, how eagerly the proconsul was drinking in the word, and fearing a dismissal. (Compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">2Ti 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen30567" type="x-p"/>
entries.3159a022e2208f6e6817868d86288058453eaf76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15869"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.13.13-Acts.13.52">Ac 13:13-52</reference>. At Perga John Mark Forsakes Them--At Antioch in Pisidia, Paul Preaches with Glorious Effect--The Jews, Enraged, Expel Them Out of Them Coasts.</title> <div sID="gen30578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15869"/><hi type="bold">13. they came to Perga in Pamphylia--</hi>The distance from Paphos to Attalia, on the Gulf of Pamphylia (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.14.25">Ac 14:25</reference>), sailing in a northwest direction, is not much greater than from Seleucia to Salamis on the east. Perga was the metropolis of Pamphylia, on the river Cestrus, and about seven miles inland from Attalia.<div eID="gen30578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and John departing from them returned to Jerusalem--</hi>As Paul afterwards peremptorily refused to take Mark with him on his second missionary journey, because he "had departed [or 'fallen off'] from them and had not gone with them to the work" (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.38">Ac 15:38</reference>), there can be no doubt that he had either wearied of it or been deterred by the prospect of the dangers which lay before him. (But see on <reference osisRef="Acts.15.37">Ac 15:37</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen30579" type="x-p"/>
entries.abd52a10373a481d60a14de0e0090af529ff4388: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15870"/><div sID="gen30580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15870"/><hi type="bold">14. departed from Perga--</hi>apparently without making any stay or doing any work: compare the different language of <reference osisRef="Acts.14.25">Ac 14:25</reference>, and see immediately below.<div eID="gen30580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came to Antioch in Pisidia--</hi>usually so called, to distinguish it from Antioch in Syria, from which they had started, though it actually lies in Phrygia, and almost due north from Perga. It was a long journey, and as it lay almost entirely through rugged mountain passes, while "rivers burst out at the base of huge cliffs, or dash down wildly through narrow ravines," it must have been a perilous one. The whole region was, and to this day is, infested by robbers, as ancient history and modern travels abundantly attest; and there can be but little doubt that to this very journey Paul many years after alludes, when he speaks amidst his "journeyings often," of his "perils of rivers" (as the word is), and his "perils of robbers" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.26">2Co 11:26</reference>). If this journey were taken in May--and earlier than that the passes would have been blocked up with snow--it would account for their not staying at Perga, whose hot streets are then deserted; "men, women, and children, flocks, herds, camels, and asses, all ascending at the beginning of the hot season from the plains to the cool basin-like hollows on the mountains, moving in the same direction with our missionaries" [Howson]. <div eID="gen30581" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c1388e6596fd41215c25c8c54b57e230a1dc554: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15871"/><div sID="gen30582" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15871"/><hi type="bold">15-17. Then Paul stood up, and beckoning with his hand--</hi>as was his manner on such occasions (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.40">Ac 21:40</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Acts.26.1">Ac 26:1</reference>).<div eID="gen30582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30583" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Men of Israel, and ye that fear God--</hi>by the latter expression meaning religious proselytes, who united with the Jews in all acts of ordinary worship.<div eID="gen30583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in Egypt--</hi>by marvellous interpositions for them in their deepest depression. <div eID="gen30584" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3b70b38530c63655fe79eced1fd0fc616bf1560: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15872"/><div sID="gen30585" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15872"/><hi type="bold">18-22. forty years suffered he their manners--</hi>rather, according to what appears the true reading, "cherished he them" (as a nurse the infant in her bosom). <div eID="gen30585" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e4f25acd1af2ef396021728fbcc26873a1dc59a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15876"/><div sID="gen30590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15876"/><hi type="bold">23-25. Of this man's seed hath God, according to ... promise, raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus--</hi>The emphasis on this statement lies: (1) in the seed from which Christ sprang--David's--and the promise to that effect, which was thus fulfilled; (2) on the character in which this promised Christ was given of God--"a Saviour." His personal name "Jesus" is emphatically added, as designed to express that very character. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Mt 1:21</reference>). <div eID="gen30590" type="x-p"/>
entries.66565f9b5092371e6ad1ef019b7583495771975e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15877"/><div sID="gen30591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15877"/><hi type="bold">26-31. children ... of Abraham, and whosoever among you feareth God--</hi>Gentile proselytes.<div eID="gen30591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to you is the word of this salvation sent--</hi>both being regarded as one class, as "the Jew first," to whom the Gospel was to be addressed in the first instance. <div eID="gen30592" type="x-p"/>
entries.19a8a13fa0bba9ad0a29eb6a25762c1aebd792e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15882"/><div sID="gen30597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15882"/><hi type="bold">33. God hath fulfilled the same--</hi>"hath completely fulfilled."<div eID="gen30597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in that he hath raised up Jesus again--</hi>literally, "raised up"; but the meaning is (notwithstanding the contrary opinion of many excellent interpreters) "from the dead"; as the context plainly shows.<div eID="gen30598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it is written in the second psalm--</hi>in many manuscripts "the first Psalm"; what we call the first being regarded by the ancient Jews as only an introduction to the Psalter, which was considered to begin with the second.<div eID="gen30599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this day have I begotten thee--</hi>As the apostle in <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference> regards the resurrection of Christ merely as the manifestation of a prior Sonship, which he afterwards (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.32">Ac 8:32</reference>) represents as essential, it is plain that this is his meaning here. (Such declarative meaning of the verb "to be" is familiar to every reader of the Bible). See <reference osisRef="John.15.8">Joh 15:8</reference>, "So shall ye be," that is, be seen to be "My disciples." It is against the whole sense of the New Testament to ascribe the origin of Christ's Sonship to His resurrection. <div eID="gen30600" type="x-p"/>
entries.23410677a5011c42c5017e6cab767dd77537ff83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15883"/><div sID="gen30601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15883"/><hi type="bold">34-37. now no more to return to corruption--</hi>that is, to the grave where death reigns; and compare <reference osisRef="Rom.6.9">Ro 6:9</reference>, "Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more, death hath no more dominion over him."<div eID="gen30601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30602" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will give you the sure mercies of David--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>). The word rendered "mercies" is peculiar, denoting the sanctity of them, as comprehending the whole riches of the new covenant; while the other word, "sure," points to the certainty with which they would, through David's Seed, be at length all substantiated. See on <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>. But how do these words prove the resurrection of Christ? "They presuppose it; for since an eternal kingdom was promised to David, the Ruler of this kingdom could not remain under the power of death. But to strengthen the indefinite prediction by one more definite, the apostle adduces <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference>, of which Peter had given the same explanation (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.2.27">Ac 2:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>, 31), both apostles denying the possibility of its proper reference to David" [Olshausen]. <div eID="gen30602" type="x-p"/>
entries.82111e7725ba4d752f03bc7b73c6867b190df104: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15885"/><div sID="gen30604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15885"/><hi type="bold">38-41. the forgiveness of sins--</hi>the first necessity of the sinner, and so the first experienced blessing of the Gospel. <div eID="gen30604" type="x-p"/>
entries.12cb0210b7ba7c7a579a635dd015b404cc09065d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15889"/><div sID="gen30609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15889"/><hi type="bold">42-43. And when the Jews were gone out of the synagogue, the Gentiles besought that these words might be preached to them the next sabbath--</hi>rather (according to what is beyond doubt the true reading), "Now, as they were going out [of the synagogue], they besought"--that is, not the Gentiles, whose case comes in afterwards, but the mixed congregation of Jews and proselytes, to whom the discourse had been addressed, entreated to have another hearing of such truths; those of them, that is, who had been impressed. "And after the breaking up of the synagogue, many of" both classes, Jews and religious; proselytes, followed Paul and Barnabas (observe, from this time forward, the inverted order of these names; except <reference osisRef="Acts.14.14">Ac 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.7">13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.25">12:25</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Acts.14.14">Ac 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.7">Ac 13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.25">Ac 12:25</reference>). These names evidently been won to the Gospel by what they had heard, and felt a clinging to their spiritual benefactors. <div eID="gen30609" type="x-p"/>
entries.96fca88b2d9dc6aa02f8d08e3e03cc8dc32d3c3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15891"/><div sID="gen30612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15891"/><hi type="bold">44-48. the next sabbath came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God--</hi>the intervening days having been spent in further inquiry and instruction, and the excitement reaching the Gentiles, who now for the first time crowded, along with the usual worshippers, into the synagogue. <div eID="gen30612" type="x-p"/>
entries.1282447db285fe6f0793812eab2fda29253d04b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15896"/><div sID="gen30624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15896"/><hi type="bold">49-52. And the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region--</hi>implying some stay in Antioch and missionary activity in its vicinity. <div eID="gen30624" type="x-p"/>

entries.91a7ff16a2b3c8d0bf4d3c0a568a097e7908f2a4: <div eID="gen44383" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen44384" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen44385" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen44385" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen44384" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen44386" type="x-p"/> Of the prophets and teachers in the Church of Antioch, <reference osisRef="Act.13.1">Act 13:1</reference>. By command of the Holy Spirit the Church appoints Saul and Barnabas to a particular work, <reference osisRef="Act.13.2">Act 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.3">Act 13:3</reference>. They depart, and travel to Seleucia, Cyprus, and Salamis, preaching in the Jewish synagogues, <reference osisRef="Act.13.4">Act 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.5">Act 13:5</reference>. At Paphos they meet with Bar-Jesus or Elymas, a Jewish sorcerer, who endeavored to prevent the deputy of the island from receiving the Christian faith, <reference osisRef="Act.13.6-Act.13.8">Act 13:6-8</reference>. Saul, for the first time called Paul, denounces the judgments of God upon him, and he is struck blind, <reference osisRef="Act.13.9-Act.13.11">Act 13:9-11</reference>. The deputy, seeing this, is confirmed in the faith, <reference osisRef="Act.13.12">Act 13:12</reference>. Paul and his company leave Paphos, and come to Pamphylia, where John Mark leaves them, and returns to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Act.13.13">Act 13:13</reference>. Paul and Barnabas proceed to Antioch; and, coming into a synagogue of the Jews, are requested by the rulers of it to preach to the people, <reference osisRef="Act.13.14">Act 13:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.15">Act 13:15</reference>. Paul preaches, and proves that Jesus is the Christ, vv. 16-41. The Gentiles desire the sermon to be preached to them the next Sabbath, and many of the Jews and proselytes receive the Christian faith, <reference osisRef="Act.13.42">Act 13:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.43">Act 13:43</reference>. The next Sabbath the whole city attend; and the Jews, filled with envy, contradict and blaspheme, <reference osisRef="Act.13.44">Act 13:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.45">Act 13:45</reference>. Paul and Barnabas with great boldness show that, by the order of God, the Gospel was to be preached first to them; but, seeing they had rejected it, it should now be taken from them, and sent to the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Act.13.46">Act 13:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.47">Act 13:47</reference>. The Gentiles rejoice and receive the truth, <reference osisRef="Act.13.48">Act 13:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.49">Act 13:49</reference>. The Jews raise a persecution against the apostles, and expel them, <reference osisRef="Act.13.50">Act 13:50</reference>. They come to Iconium, full of joy and the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="Act.13.51">Act 13:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.13.52">Act 13:52</reference>. <div eID="gen44386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44387" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen44387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44388" type="x-p"/> Certain prophets and teachers - Προφηται και διδασκαλοι. It is probable that these were not distinct offices; both might be vested in the same persons. By prophets we are to understand, when the word is taken simply, persons who were frequently inspired to predict future events, and by teachers, persons whose ordinary office was to instruct the people in the Christian doctrine. These also, to be properly qualified for the office, must have been endued with the influence of the Holy Spirit; for, as but a very small portion of the Scriptures of the New Testament could have as yet been given, it was necessary that the teachers should derive much of their own teaching by immediate revelation from God. On prophets and teachers, see the note on <reference osisRef="Act.11.27">Act 11:27</reference>. <div eID="gen44388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44389" type="x-p"/> Barnabas - Of whom see before, <reference osisRef="Act.11.22-Act.11.24">Act 11:22-24</reference>. <div eID="gen44389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44390" type="x-p"/> Simeon-Niger - Or Simeon the Black, either because of his complexion, or his hair. It was on reasons of this kind that surnames, surnoms, name upon name were first imposed. Of this Simeon nothing farther is known. <div eID="gen44390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44391" type="x-p"/> Lucius of Cyrene - See <reference osisRef="Act.11.20">Act 11:20</reference>. <div eID="gen44391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44392" type="x-p"/> Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod - Our margin has given the proper meaning of the original word συντροφος, a foster-brother; i.e. Manaen was the son of the woman who nursed Herod Antipas; and the son, also, whose milk the young Herod shared. Of a person whose name was Manaen or Menahem, and who was in the court of Herod, we read several things in the Jewish writers. They say that this man had the gift of prophecy, and that he told Herod, when he was but a child, that he would be king. When Herod became king he sent for him to his court, and held him in great estimation. It might have been the son of this Menahem of whom St. Luke here speaks. Dr. Lightfoot has shown this to be at least possible.
entries.36c22731052ad57ca87cd50d41d4b0d63e6c57f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen44392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44393" type="x-p"/> As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted - On Mondays and Thursdays it was usual with the more pious Jews to attend the public service in their synagogues, and to fast: the former is what we are to understand by ministering to the Lord. On the Sabbaths they attended the service in the synagogue, but did not fast. The Greek word, λειτουργουντων, signifies performing the office of praying, supplicating, rendering thanks, etc.: hence the word λειτουργια, liturgy, the work of prayer, etc., from λιτη, supplication, according to some; or rather from λειτος, common, and εργον, work, the common or public work, in which all the people were engaged. <div eID="gen44393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44394" type="x-p"/> The Holy Ghost said - A revelation of the Divine will was made to some person then present; probably to either Simeon, or Lucius, or Manaen, mentioned before. <div eID="gen44394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44395" type="x-p"/> Separate me Barnabas and Saul - Consecrate, or set them apart, for the particular work whereunto I have called them. How this was done, we find in the next verse.
entries.63c2b846fba8cd85a038c9fb15b96d4ead825b78: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen44395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44396" type="x-p"/> And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them - <div eID="gen44396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44397" type="x-p"/> 1. They fasted: this was probably done by the whole Church. <div eID="gen44397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44398" type="x-p"/> 2.
